entries.title: Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
entries.summary: Large training jobs can stall or compute wrong results even when every node looks healthy. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now adds workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks that catch these failures sooner and raise the goodput of your training workloads.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod

Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy. A GPU with a subtle fault can pass its stress tests and still return wrong values. When a job stalls on an NCCL timeout, it keeps its GPUs, and Slurm still shows it as running. If a device plugin crashes on one node, the job fails with an error that never mentions the plugin. Teams usually find these problems only after the loss diverges or the job fails, and by then the compute is spent. Each of these failures lowers goodput, the share of your cluster’s time that goes to useful training. Today, we’re introducing workload recovery and infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod that catch these failures sooner and raise the goodput of your training workloads.

SageMaker HyperPod already handles nodes that report hardware faults. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors, deep health checks test nodes during provisioning, and automatic node recovery reboots or replaces faulty hardware. These features look at one node’s hardware at a time. They can’t tell whether the GPUs train correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the Kubernetes components a job depends on are working.

In this post, we walk through the three new capabilities that catch these failures. For each one, we show how to set it up and what it reports when it finds a problem:

  • MultiNodeTrainingValidation
    is a new deep health check for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When HyperPod provisions an instance, or when you run the check on demand, it trains a small model on the instance and then across instances of the same type. The instance fails if the loss becomes NaN or infinite, or training doesn’t finish in time.
  • The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the Kubernetes layer of an EKS cluster for problems such as crash-looping device plugins, missing DaemonSets, and tainted nodes. When a job fails, it reports the pods and nodes involved as Kubernetes events and Amazon CloudWatch logs.
  • Hung job detection finds Slurm jobs that have stopped making progress. An agent on each node watches the job’s output and GPU activity, or log patterns that you define. It writes an event to CloudWatch and can cancel the job so that Slurm requeues it.

Why node health alone isn’t enough

The existing HyperPod resiliency features check a single node at a time. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors such as Xid and NVLink faults, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) errors, and kernel errors. The InstanceStress deep health check runs DCGM level 4 diagnostics and tests each instance’s GPUs, GPU memory, NVLink, and EFA devices. The InstanceConnectivity check runs NCCL tests across GPU instances, or NCCOM tests on AWS Trainium. Together, these confirm that each node’s hardware works. They don’t show whether the GPUs compute correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the cluster’s Kubernetes components are healthy. Three kinds of failure get past them:

  • Numerical faults – A GPU can pass every hardware test and still compute wrong results. The first sign is often NaN or infinite loss in a production run. Meta attributed 6 of the 419 unexpected interruptions in its 54-day Llama 3 405B pre-training run to silent data corruption (The Llama 3 Herd of Models).
  • Hung jobs – An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can stop a job without ending it. The job keeps its GPUs and their memory, and Slurm reports it as running until someone checks the loss curve or the log.
  • Cluster-level failures – Some failures happen in Kubernetes, not in a node’s hardware. A device plugin crash-loops, a required DaemonSet never starts on a new node, or ranks on different nodes fall out of step in an NCCL collective. HMA checks each node on its own, so it doesn’t see these problems. When the job fails, the error often doesn’t say which pod or node caused it.

Solution overview

Each capability covers a different point in a training run. 

MultiNodeTrainingValidation
runs when instances are provisioned, or on demand, and confirms that their GPUs train correctly. Hung job detection runs alongside each Slurm job and catches a job that has stopped making progress. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the cluster continuously and, when a job fails, reports the pods and nodes that were involved. The following table summarizes the three.
CapabilityWhat it catchesWhen it runsAvailable on
MultiNodeTrainingValidation
deep health check		 NaN or infinite loss, or training that doesn’t finish in time, on GPUs that pass hardware checksWhen instances are created or updated, or on demandEKS clusters, on supported EFA-enabled NVIDIA GPU instances
HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring AgentNode condition changes, pod and DaemonSet failures, and failed training jobs, with the pods and nodes involved. NCCL communication state for jobs that opt inContinuouslyEKS clusters
Hung job detectionJobs that stop making progress but don’t exitWhile each job runsSlurm clusters

Hung job detection is new for Slurm clusters. On EKS clusters, HyperPod already detects hung jobs that run through the HyperPod training operator, and Ray Train jobs get hang detection by default. We describe both options in the hung job detection section.

Each capability targets a different source of lost goodput. Scheduling goodput is the share of time that all the resources a job needs are available. Runtime goodput is the share of that time in which the job makes forward progress. Program goodput is the share of the hardware’s peak performance that the job gets. The following table shows the effect of each capability.

CapabilityScheduling goodputRuntime goodputProgram goodput
MultiNodeTrainingValidation
 Instances that fail the training test are labeled and, with automatic node recovery, replaced, so jobs don’t start on hardware that produces invalid outputFewer production runs lost to NaN or infinite loss from a faulty GPUFlags instances whose training doesn’t finish within the time limit
HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring AgentReports nodes that lose GPUs or EFA devices, missing device plugins, and taints, so you can restore capacity soonerNames the pods and nodes behind a failed job, so you find the cause and restart soonerNo direct effect
Hung job detectionNo direct effectFlags a hung job in minutes instead of hours, and can cancel it so Slurm requeues itNo direct effect

Consider a pre-training job running on 32 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (256 NVIDIA H100 GPUs). If the job hangs at 1:00 AM and no one notices until 9:00 AM, it wastes 256 instance-hours or 2,048 GPU-hours. At the SageMaker HyperPod on-demand price of approximately $66 per instance-hour in US East (N. Virginia), the hang costs about $16,900. With a 15-minute hung job detection rule, HyperPod cancels the stalled job and Slurm requeues it. The hang costs about $530 instead, saving approximately $16,400.

Validate training correctness with the 
MultiNodeTrainingValidation
deep health check

The 

MultiNodeTrainingValidation
deep health check trains a fixed, known-good workload, first on each instance and then across instances. It catches GPUs that pass InstanceStress and InstanceConnectivity but produce NaN or infinite loss once they train together. If an instance fails, HyperPod labels it as failed and, with automatic node recovery turned on, reboots or replaces it. When the check runs during provisioning, this happens before your jobs can use the instance.

How it works

MultiNodeTrainingValidation
adds two tests to the deep health check run:
  • Tiny Megatron test: A short Megatron-LM training run on all GPUs of each instance.
  • Megatron test: The same workload across instances of the same type, communicating over EFA.

Either test fails an instance if the training loss becomes NaN or infinite, or if training doesn’t finish within the time limit. The workload is fixed, so a failure points to the hardware rather than to a model or code change.

The following table shows how it fits with the other deep health checks.

CheckWhat it runsWhat it catches
InstanceStress
 GPU and NVLink count, DCGM level 4 diagnostics, and EFA latency and bandwidth tests (Neuron tests on Trainium)Hardware that’s missing, failing, or unstable
InstanceConnectivity
 NCCL tests across GPU instances (NCCOM on Trainium)Slow or broken communication between instances
MultiNodeTrainingValidation
 Tiny Megatron test on each instance, Megatron test across instancesGPUs that run but train incorrectly: NaN or infinite loss, or training that doesn’t finish in time

Prerequisites

You need the following:

  • An Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS.
  • An instance group of a supported EFA-enabled NVIDIA GPU instance type, such as ml.p5.48xlarge. The Megatron test runs across instances of the same type.

Turn on MultiNodeTrainingValidation for an instance group

HyperPod runs deep health checks when it creates or updates instances. To include 

MultiNodeTrainingValidation
, add it to 
OnStartDeepHealthChecks
in the instance group configuration that you pass to 
create-cluster
or 
update-cluster
. We turned on all three checks:

To confirm the setting, run the following command:

The output lists the three checks:

Run MultiNodeTrainingValidation on demand

You can also check instances that are already in the cluster, for example before a long pre-training run. Use the 

StartClusterHealthCheck
API:

To check specific instances instead of the whole group, add 

"InstanceIds": [...]
to the configuration.

Check the results

HyperPod writes one line per test to the 

DeepHealthCheckResults/
log stream in your cluster’s CloudWatch log group, 
/aws/sagemaker/Clusters//
. Here’s the stream from our run on two ml.p5.48xlarge instances. 
TINY_MEGATRON
and 
MEGATRON
are the two 
MultiNodeTrainingValidation
tests:

When the run finishes, each instance carries the result as a node label:

For the training details, read 

/var/log/aws/clusters/sagemaker-deep-health-check.log
on the instance, for example through an AWS Systems Manager session. On the instance that ran rank 0, the log ends with a summary of the Megatron test:

The other instance’s log has a line for every iteration, with the loss and a running count of NaN iterations:

In our run, the loss fell from 11.57 to 3.62 over 300 iterations, with no NaN or skipped iterations, at about 507 milliseconds per iteration on 16 H100 GPUs.

How long MultiNodeTrainingValidation takes

On our two-node cluster, the full deep health check took 1 hour 28 minutes after the instances finished their lifecycle scripts. DCGM level 4 diagnostics took most of that. The two 

MultiNodeTrainingValidation
tests added about 8 minutes. Instances can’t take workloads until the checks finish, so plan for this additional time when you add capacity.

Keep in mind that 

MultiNodeTrainingValidation
tests the hardware with a fixed reference workload. A pass means the instances trained that workload correctly. It doesn’t guarantee that your own job will converge. We recommend running it on new capacity, on replacement instances, and before long pre-training runs.

Catch cluster-level failures with the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent

HMA watches the hardware on each node, but many failures that stop a training job happen in Kubernetes. A device plugin can crash-loop until its node stops offering GPUs to the scheduler, or a taint can evict a job’s pods. The job error rarely names the pod or node involved, so engineers piece together what happened from kubectl output, per-rank logs, and timestamps.

The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches these resources from one place in the cluster. When something breaks, it tells you what changed and which nodes, pods, and jobs are affected. It reports through Kubernetes events and structured CloudWatch logs. The agent only reports. It doesn’t reboot nodes or restart jobs, because the cause might be in the workload. HMA and HyperPod node recovery still handle hardware faults, and the HyperPod training operator still handles job restarts.

How the agent works

The agent runs as a single pod per cluster in the aws-hyperpod namespace and prefers CPU nodes, so it doesn’t use GPU capacity. It watches the following:

  • Nodes: The agent reports these changes:
    • Condition changes such as 
      NotReady
      or memory, disk, or PID pressure.
    • Fewer allocatable GPUs or EFA devices.
    • Lost NVIDIA capability labels.
    • Added, changed, or removed taints.
    • Missing HyperPod labels.
  • Critical infrastructure pods: DaemonSet pods in kube-system, aws-hyperpod, and kubeflow, plus the training operator’s controller. The agent reports crash loops, restarts, container errors, and pods that stay not ready.
  • DaemonSets: Required DaemonSets that are missing or have no available pods, rollouts that stall, and pods running on nodes that no longer allow them.
  • Training jobs: HyperPodPyTorchJob, Kubeflow PyTorchJob (v1), and Kubeflow TrainJob (v2). When a job fails, the agent records the failure reason with the job’s pods and nodes.
  • NCCL communication: For jobs that opt in, the state of the job’s NCCL communicators, read from NCCL’s built-in reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) subsystem.

The agent reports what it finds in two places:

  • Kubernetes events on the affected node, pod, DaemonSet, or job. A Warning event marks a problem and a Normal event marks its recovery. You read them with kubectl get events and kubectl describe.
  • Structured JSON logs in the cluster’s CloudWatch log group, which keep the history after Kubernetes events expire.

The following table lists the events you’re most likely to see.

Event reasonRaised when
TrainingJobFailedA HyperPodPyTorchJob or Kubeflow job fails. The message includes the failure reason from the job’s operator.
CriticalPodCrashLoop, CriticalPodRestartedA device plugin, HMA, or another critical pod crash-loops or restarts.
NecessaryDaemonSetMissingA DaemonSet you declared as required is missing or has no available pods.
NodeResourceDegradedA node’s allocatable GPUs or EFA devices drop or disappear.
NodeConditionDegradedA node becomes NotReady or reports memory, disk, or PID pressure.
NodeTaintAdded, NoExecuteTaintAppliedA node is tainted. For a NoExecute taint, the log lists the pods and jobs that might be evicted.
DaemonSetMisscheduledDaemonSet pods are running on nodes that no longer allow them.
NodeRecovered, PodRecovered, DaemonSetRecoveredA problem reported earlier has cleared.

For the full list of events, see the documentation.

Prerequisites

You need the following:

  • A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS.
  • For an existing cluster, kubectl and Helm access to the cluster, and the HyperPod Helm chart from the sagemaker-hyperpod-cli repository.
  • NCCL 2.24 or later in the training container, if you want to monitor NCCL communication.

Install and verify the agent

If your cluster already uses the HyperPod Helm chart, apply the agent’s custom resource definition (CRD) first, because Helm doesn’t install CRDs during an upgrade. Then upgrade the release with the agent turned on:

The upgrade also moves the other HyperPod components in the chart, such as HMA and the device plugins, to the chart’s current versions. To see what will change first, run the same command with 

--dry-run=server
.

Check that the agent is running and that its health report exists:

The health report lists the HyperPod components that the agent tracks, such as HMA, and when their status last changed:

By default, HMA is the only required DaemonSet. If your cluster uses the device plugins from the HyperPod Helm chart, add them so that the agent reports a missing plugin. Also add the namespaces where your training jobs run, so that it can link pod failures to their jobs. Each list replaces its default, so keep the default entries. Save the following as 

krma-values.yaml
:

Then apply it:

See what the agent reports

To see how the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent handles an infrastructure failure, we deployed a small DaemonSet into aws-hyperpod, pinned it to one node, and made it exit a few seconds after starting. It behaves like a crash-looping device plugin without touching the real one. Within seconds, the agent raised events on the pod and the DaemonSet:

Next, we ran a two-node HyperPodPyTorchJob and made one rank exit during training. The agent raised a TrainingJobFailed event on the job:

It also wrote the failure to CloudWatch with the pods and nodes involved, so you don’t need to look them up from the job’s pod list:

The agent writes these logs to the cluster log group, 

/aws/sagemaker/Clusters//
, in streams named 
SageMakerClusterMonitoringAgent//
. It starts a new stream when it moves to another node, so filter by the stream prefix. For sample queries, see the documentation.

Monitor NCCL communication for a job

NCCL 2.24 and later include the reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) subsystem, a small listener in each NCCL process that reports the state of the job’s communicators. For jobs that opt in, the agent reads this report from every pod every 30 seconds.

By default, NCCL binds the RAS listener to 

localhost
inside the pod, where the agent can’t reach it. To opt a job in, you bind the listener to the pod IP instead. That makes port 28028 reachable on the pod network, which NVIDIA’s documentation notes has security implications. Before you turn it on, apply a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that allows TCP port 28028 only from the agent’s pod and still allows traffic between the job’s own pods. The agent’s documentation includes an example policy. Then set 
NCCL_RAS_ADDR
in the training container:

To confirm the setting, turn on NCCL debug logging with 

NCCL_DEBUG=INFO
and 
NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,RAS
. Each rank then logs the address RAS listens on:

If the address is 

::1
or 
127.0.0.1
, 
NCCL_RAS_ADDR
isn’t set and the agent can’t reach the listener.

For each monitored job, the agent combines the per-pod results into a job-level state. The job is healthy when every pod returns a valid report, degraded when only some do, and unhealthy when none do. Unhealthy usually means the training processes have stopped.

The agent logs a summary after each polling cycle. In a run on two ml.p5.48xlarge instances, every cycle reported both training pods healthy, 30 seconds apart:

The agent also writes each RAS report to CloudWatch, so you can spot communicator problems while the job is still running. In our test, we made one rank of a two-node job stop calling 

all_reduce
. The report from the next polling cycle showed the communicator out of step and named the rank, GPU, process, and node that had fallen behind:

Rank 1 is one operation behind rank 0, so start with rank 1’s GPU on node 10.0.2.22.

Detect and recover hung jobs on HyperPod Slurm clusters

A training job can hang without exiting. An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can leave the job holding its GPUs while Slurm still shows it as running. It stays that way until someone notices that the loss or the log has stopped changing. Teams that run Slurm often build their own watchdog scripts and alarms to catch these jobs, and then need to maintain them.

Today, we’re launching hung job detection for SageMaker HyperPod Slurm clusters. It finds these jobs, writes an event to CloudWatch, and can cancel a hung job so that Slurm puts it back in the queue. You turn it on for each job with an environment variable that points to a small rules file. It needs no changes to your training scripts or containers, and it works with PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, and custom scripts.

How hung job detection works

Hung job detection runs as an agent on every node and is off by default. The agent watches only jobs that set the 

HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES
environment variable to the path of a rules file. The rules file decides how the agent detects a hang:
  • Default detection watches the job’s standard output and GPU activity. It declares a hang when the output stops for an extended period while the GPUs sit idle but still hold memory. That’s what a rendezvous hang looks like, when one node fails and the others wait at a barrier. It also declares a hang when the output stops for a longer period, whatever the GPUs are doing. In our test, the first case fired 15 minutes after the job’s last output.
  • Custom rules watch your log for regular expressions that you choose. A progress rule declares a hang when a line such as your training step message doesn’t appear within its timeout. An error rule declares a hang as soon as a line such as an NCCL error appears. Custom rules replace default detection for that job.
Default detectionCustom rules
Turn on with{“enabled”: true}One or more enabled log_pattern rules
Declares a hang whenOutput stops while GPUs are idle but hold memory, or output stops for a longer periodA progress pattern doesn’t appear within its timeout, or an error pattern appears
MissesJobs that keep their GPUs busy without making progress, such as a job stuck in a loopHangs your patterns don’t describe. If a pattern keeps matching, no hang is declared, even with idle GPUs

When the agent declares a hang, it writes a 

HANG_DETECTED
event to CloudWatch. If the rules file sets the action to 
cancel
, the agent also cancels the job and Slurm requeues it. With the default action, 
notify
, the agent writes the event and leaves the job running.

Hung job detection is separate from auto-resume, which restarts jobs that exit after a hardware failure. Auto-resume handles jobs that crash and hung job detection handles jobs that keep running without making progress.

On HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS, HyperPod already detects hung jobs in two cases. The HyperPod training operator checks the logs of each HyperPodPyTorchJob against rules in the job specification and restarts the job when it hangs. The same rules can also restart a job whose throughput drops or whose loss spikes. You don’t need Ray for this. For Ray Train jobs, HyperPod hung job detection for Ray watches every worker by default, with no changes to your code.

Prerequisites

You need the following:

  • A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Slurm.
  • A HyperPod Slurm AMI released on or after November 10, 2026, which includes hung job detection. Clusters created on or after that date already have it. To check an existing cluster without updating it, run 
    srun --help
    on a cluster node. If the output lists 
    --no-hang-detection
    , the cluster supports hung job detection. If it doesn’t, update the cluster software first. The update replaces each instance’s root volume, so back up anything stored there before you update.
  • A rules file that every compute node in the job can read at the same path. The agent reads the file from that path on each node. Shared storage such as Amazon FSx for Lustre or Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) is a straightforward option. To keep rules files in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), copy them to the same path on every node, for example in your lifecycle script. If you plan to use a directory such as 
    /opt/slurm
    , first confirm that it’s shared across nodes rather than local to each one.

Turn on hung job detection

Create a rules file on shared storage. The smallest valid file turns on default detection:

The agent uses whatever rules file a job points to and doesn’t check who owns it. Anyone who can edit the file, or replace it in its directory, can change detection for every job that uses it, including making the agent cancel those jobs. The 

chmod 600
in the example keeps a personal rules file private to its owner. For a file that a team shares, use 
chmod 644
so the team can read it and only its maintainer can edit it. In both cases, make the parent directory writable only by its owner so nobody can swap the file.

Then point the job at the rules file when you submit it:

To use one rules file for many jobs, you can also set 

HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES
in a shell profile or a site-wide profile script.

When a monitored job starts, the first lines of its output show that the agent registered it:

These lines also appear when the rules file is invalid, so check CloudWatch for a 

CONFIG_ERROR
event too, as described in the next section.

Add custom rules to track training progress

Default detection can’t catch a job that keeps its GPUs busy without making progress, so we recommend at least one rule that watches for your training steps or epochs. The following rules file cancels the job if no epoch finishes for 45 minutes, or as soon as an NCCL error appears:

The fields work as follows:

  • Set enabled to true on each rule. Rules are off by default.
  • start_timeout_minutes
    is how long the job can run before the pattern first appears. Set it longer than the time your job needs to load the model, compile, and restore a checkpoint.
  • timeout_minutes
    is how long the pattern can stay absent after that. Set it longer than the biggest normal gap, including checkpoint saves and evaluation.
  • stop_pattern
    turns the rule off when it matches, so work after training ends isn’t flagged.
  • fault_on_match
    marks an error pattern. One match means the job is hung.

By default, the agent reads the job’s Slurm output file. To watch a different file, set 

monitoring.log_file
. To cut false positives, set 
metric_evaluation_data_points
on a rule so that several 10-second checks in a row must fail before the agent declares a hang. A rules file can have up to 20 rules and be up to 1 MB.

Start with 

"action": "notify"
while you tune timeouts and patterns, and switch to 
cancel
once the events match real hangs.

View hung job detection events in CloudWatch

HyperPod writes detection events from the controller node to the cluster’s CloudWatch log group, 

/aws/sagemaker/Clusters//
, in the stream 
SageMakerHangJobDetectionEvents//
. Events for every job land in this stream, whichever node the job ran on. To find the events for one job, filter by its job ID:

We tested each detection method on a HyperPod Slurm cluster with two ml.p5.48xlarge instances. The first test job allocated GPU memory and then stopped producing output. Default detection flagged it 15 minutes after its last output:

The 

layer
field shows which method fired: 
signal_evaluator
for default detection, or 
pattern_evaluator
for a custom rule. In a second test, a progress rule with a 2-minute timeout fired 2 minutes after the job’s last step. In a third, an error rule fired about one second after the job printed an NCCL error line. Because that rules file used cancel, the agent also wrote a 
HANG_ACTION_TAKEN
event with the action Slurm took (we’ve left out the time, level, and msg fields):

Slurm put the job back in the queue, and the requeued run started about 2.5 minutes later. 

sacct
shows both runs:

Slurm requeues a job up to the cluster’s 

MaxBatchRequeue
limit, which was 5 on our cluster. A job submitted with 
#SBATCH --no-requeue
reported 
"action": "cancel"
instead and stayed canceled. With 
notify
, there’s no 
HANG_ACTION_TAKEN
event. The agent follows 
HANG_DETECTED
with a record that says 
Hang notification sent, no automatic action taken
.

If a rules file is missing or invalid, the agent doesn’t monitor the job and writes a 

CONFIG_ERROR
event instead. Here’s the event for a rules file with a JSON syntax error:

The job ran to completion without monitoring, and nothing appeared in 

sbatch
, 
squeue
, or the job’s output. Test a new rules file with a short job and check for this event before you use it for production jobs.

With notify, the job keeps running until someone acts on the event. To get an alert, create a CloudWatch metric filter for 

HANG_DETECTED
events and an alarm that notifies an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic:

Turn off hung job detection

To turn off detection for a job that would otherwise inherit 

HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES
, add 
--no-hang-detection
to 
srun
, or to 
sbatch
to cover every step in the job. To turn it off for every job that uses a rules file, set 
"enabled": false
in the file. Running jobs keep their current settings, and the change applies to jobs you submit afterward.

Conclusion

Node health is essential to reliable distributed training, but it does not provide a complete picture of workload health. 

MultiNodeTrainingValidation
detects instances that pass hardware diagnostics but produce invalid training results. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent connects Kubernetes infrastructure failures to the jobs, pods, and nodes involved. Hung job detection identifies Slurm jobs that remain active after they stop making progress and can return them to the queue automatically.

Together, these capabilities help you detect failures earlier, shorten investigations, and raise goodput by reducing the GPU time spent on workloads that can’t make useful progress. Use 

MultiNodeTrainingValidation
when adding or revalidating capacity, run the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent continuously on supported Amazon EKS clusters, and begin hung job detection in notify mode before you switch to automatic cancellation. To get started, see the SageMaker HyperPod resiliency documentation for Amazon EKS and the hung job detection documentation for Slurm. To learn more, visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod product page.

entries.title: Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard
entries.summary: The Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard compares 70+ foundation models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in SageMaker Studio. Learn what the leaderboard shows, how AWS benchmarks models, and how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard

Amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy quickly. That choice is powerful, but it also creates a real question: Which model should you start with? Comparing models usually means reading model cards one at a time and hunting for benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. Then you still must guess how each model will perform, and what it will cost, for your use case.

Today we are launching the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard, a new way to compare JumpStart models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio. In this post, we explain what the leaderboard shows, define the key terms in plain language, and walk through how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model.

What is the JumpStart Model Leaderboard?

The leaderboard is a new view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views. It uses the same search bar and filters you already know, and it opens on a leaderboard of large language models (LLMs). You see rankings immediately without answering setup questions first. For each model, it shows two kinds of information:

  • Quality scores on three public benchmarks (BIG-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro) that AWS runs itself, using the same evaluation setup for every model so the numbers are comparable.
  • Performance and cost metrics that AWS measures by sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint using each JumpStart deployment configuration, so you see how fast a model responds and what it costs to run.

Because both kinds of numbers come from the same place and the same method, you can make a like-for-like comparison instead of stitching together data from different websites. At launch, the leaderboard covers 70+ models from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee, with more added over time.

The following screenshot shows the leaderboard in SageMaker Studio, with benchmark scores, performance metrics, and estimated cost for each model.

Key concepts

This section defines the terms the leaderboard uses: the quality benchmarks, the use case profiles and optimization goals that shape the performance numbers, and the performance metrics themselves.

Quality benchmarks

A benchmark is a standardized test: a fixed set of questions with known answers. Running every model through the same test gives you a score you can compare. At launch, the leaderboard reports three reasoning benchmarks for LLMs:

BenchmarkWhat it measures, in plain terms
BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)A set of challenging tasks that require multi-step reasoning, such as logical deduction, tracking objects, and multi-step arithmetic.
GPQA DiamondGraduate-level science questions that are difficult to answer by searching the web. A good signal of deep reasoning.
MMLU-ProBroad knowledge and reasoning across many subjects, such as science, law, and engineering, using harder multiple-choice questions.

Higher is better for all three. The leaderboard shows each benchmark separately rather than blending them into one number. That keeps the results transparent: You can weigh the benchmarks that matter for your application and check each score against the public definition of the benchmark.

Use case profiles and optimization goals

Speed and cost depend on your workload and on how the model is deployed. Two menus above the leaderboard control which performance and cost numbers you see:

  • Use case profile. Select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu. The default is Max Context. The profile changes only the performance and cost metrics. Quality benchmark scores are the same for every profile.
  • Optimization goal. For each profile, a model can have several deployment configurations, and the leaderboard shows metrics for one at a time. Choose which one with the Optimized for menu. The default is Balanced.

Each optimization goal picks a different configuration:

Optimization goalConfiguration shown
BalancedThe configuration with the lowest estimated cost per token. Because cost per token depends on both instance price and throughput, this balances what you pay per hour against how fast the instance generates tokens.
Cost optimizedThe configuration with the lowest hourly instance price. Latency can be higher and throughput lower than with other goals.
Latency optimizedThe configuration with the lowest time to first token.
Throughput optimizedThe configuration with the highest throughput. These configurations can use speculative decoding.

Performance metrics

MetricWhat it tells you
Time to first token (TTFT)How long a user waits before the model starts responding. Lower is better, and it matters most for chat.
Throughput per request (tokens/s)How many tokens the model generates per second. Higher is better, and it matters for batch and high-volume workloads.
Instance cost ($/hr)The estimated cost per hour given a specified instance type.

A note on cost: Estimated cost reflects SageMaker instance cost only, based on the on-demand hourly rate for the configuration’s default instance type. It does not include data transfer, storage, inference component costs, or discounts such as Reserved Instances or AWS Savings Plans. Your actual bill will vary. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator for billing estimates.

How we benchmark

Published benchmark scores often come from different teams using different prompts, settings, and hardware, which makes them hard to compare. We took a different approach:

  • One method for every model. AWS runs each benchmark with the same evaluation harness and settings across all models on the leaderboard.
  • Measured on SageMaker. Performance and cost come from sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint deployed with each JumpStart deployment configuration, the same configurations you can launch.

For full details, including prompts, generation settings, and how configurations are measured, see JumpStart leaderboard methodology.

Walkthrough: Finding a model

The following steps show how to go from browsing to a deployed model. You need access to SageMaker Studio and permission to deploy JumpStart models.

Step 1: Open the leaderboard

In SageMaker Studio, open the Models page, then select the Leaderboard view. The leaderboard keeps the same search bar and filters as the other views, and it has its own URL. You can bookmark it or share a direct link with your team.

The following screenshot shows the Models page with the Leaderboard view selected.

Step 2: Narrow the list with filters

Use the same search and filters you already use elsewhere in JumpStart to keep only the models that fit your requirements. Common filters include license, provider, and input and output modality. Start with hard requirements, for example a license that allows commercial use, before you look at scores.

The following screenshot shows the leaderboard filtered by input modality, output modality, and license.

Step 3: Choose a use case profile and optimization goal

Above the leaderboard, select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu (default: Max Context). Then choose a goal from the Optimized for menu (default: Balanced). For a chatbot your customers interact with, Latency optimized is a sensible start. For overnight document processing, Throughput optimized or Cost optimized may fit better. The performance and cost columns update, and quality scores stay the same.

The following screenshots show the View benchmarks for your use case and Optimized for menus above the leaderboard.

Step 4: Read the heatmap and customize columns

Each column has a blue heatmap, so the top-performing models stand out at a glance: the deeper the blue, the stronger the result in that column. Sort any benchmark column to rank models by the metric you care about most. Use the column settings (gear icon) to hide metrics you don’t need, and scroll horizontally to see more. The model name columns stay frozen as you scroll, and a fade at the edge shows when more columns are available.

The following screenshot shows the heatmap and the column settings menu.

Step 5: Deploy or customize the model

Choose a model to open it. From there, you have options to deploy the model or, for models that support serverless customization, to customize it. If you deploy, choose the same use case and optimization goal you compared on the leaderboard. Each metric applies to the configuration it was measured on, and a different configuration can change quality, latency, throughput, and cost.

The following screenshot shows a model page with the Deploy and Customize options.

Example: Picking a model for a chat assistant

Suppose you are building an internal help-desk assistant. Employees ask questions and expect fast, accurate answers that follow a set response format. You need a commercially licensed model and want to keep costs predictable.

After filtering by license and choosing a chat-like use case profile with Latency optimized, your shortlist might look like this:

ModelBBHMMLU-ProTTFT (s)Throughput (tokens/s)Instance cost ($/hr)
Model A (large)95.987.22.3337$37.66
Model B (medium)94.284.90.9844$5.75
Model C (small)77.466.10.2761$2.61

Reading the table, Model A has the highest knowledge score but also the highest cost and the slowest first response. Model B scores almost as well, holds up on multi-step reasoning, and runs on a smaller, cheaper instance. For a help desk, where reasoning through a question and responding quickly matter more than the last few points of general knowledge, Model B is the better starting point. A bigger model is not always the better choice, and the leaderboard makes that trade-off visible in seconds.

From there, you would deploy Model B, test it with real questions from your help desk, and keep Model C in mind as a lower-cost option if quality holds up.

Tips and things to know

  • Use the leaderboard to build a shortlist, not to make the final call. Benchmarks measure general ability. Always evaluate your top two or three models on your own data and prompts before going to production.
  • Filter first, then rank. Requirements like license and input or output modality rule models in or out. Scores only help you order what is left.
  • Compare models within a benchmark. Each benchmark has its own difficulty, so a score on one benchmark isn’t directly comparable with a score on another.
  • Account for model type. Reasoning and non-reasoning models are evaluated with different generation parameters, and GPQA Diamond scores for reasoning models are averaged over 10 passes. Comparisons between the two types are approximate.
  • Check the deployment configuration. Each metric applies to the configuration it was measured on. Compare models on the configuration you plan to deploy.
  • Treat close scores as ties. Small differences can fall within normal run-to-run variation and don’t mean one model is meaningfully better. Look for clear gaps.
  • Coverage is growing. Not every JumpStart model has benchmark scores yet, and launch benchmarks focus on LLMs. A model without a score is not a weak model. It simply has not been benchmarked yet.

What’s next

We’re continuing to expand the leaderboard. Areas we’re exploring include:

  • Private hub support, so organizations that use curated JumpStart private hubs can see a leaderboard for their approved models.
  • More task leaderboards beyond LLM text generation, such as object detection, text embeddings, and image understanding.
  • More models and benchmarks as new models are added to JumpStart.

Conclusion

The SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard brings quality, speed, and cost together in one place, measured consistently on SageMaker. Instead of comparing numbers from different sources, you can filter to the models that fit your requirements, compare them on the configuration you plan to run, and deploy with a few clicks.

To get started, open the Models page in SageMaker Studio and select the Leaderboard view. To learn more, see the following resources:

Open the leaderboard, shortlist two or three models for your workload, and deploy them to test with your own prompts before you choose one for production.

entries.title: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: Airbnb runs evals on real engineering tasks and uses Amazon Bedrock observability to choose models for its coding agents and control production costs. This post shows how cost per task guides model selection, why production spending can differ from eval results, and how to monitor latency, manage quotas, and attribute spend.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure. It integrates with AWS access controls and monitoring, and processes prompts, code, and model responses within AWS.

As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost. Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics in Amazon CloudWatch help teams investigate latency increases, throttling, and changes in token consumption. Evaluations, or evals, complement these operational metrics by assessing the quality of an agent’s work on a fixed set of representative tasks.

In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock. We explain how cost per task guides model selection and how production data helps us revisit those choices as usage changes. We also describe the runtime signals used to investigate latency, throttling, and spend.

At Airbnb, thousands of engineers and engineering-adjacent people use AirChat, our internal tool for running coding agents, every week. The agents send their model requests through our large language model (LLM) gateway, which runs on Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock processes Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses within AWS. Eight new models came out in about five weeks. By mid-October, about two thirds of the requests our engineers sent through coding agents went to those new models.

Each release can change output tokens, cost, latency and capacity at once, and the benchmark charts published with a launch don’t show how a model handles our engineers’ work. So we run two systems side by side. Before a rollout, we run evals on our own tasks to measure each model’s score and cost per task. Cost per task is the list-price cost of all the tokens an agent uses to finish one task.

After a rollout, observability shows us what changed in production. When production usage doesn’t match the eval results, we find out why.

Solution overview

You can diagnose most production problems with a few signals in the 

AWS/Bedrock
namespace in CloudWatch:
  • Latency: 
    InvocationLatency
    , 
    TimeToFirstToken
    , 
    OutputTokenCount
    , and output tokens per second (OTPS), which you derive.
  • Throttling: 
    InvocationThrottles
    , plus the tokens each request reserves against your quota, which you publish yourself. Bedrock also publishes 
    EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage
    , which measures your estimated tokens per minute (TPM) quota consumption, including cache write tokens and output burndown multipliers, across all inference APIs (
    Converse
    , 
    InvokeModel
    , 
    ConverseStream
    , and 
    InvokeModelWithResponseStream
    ). You can use this metric to set proactive alarms before reaching your quota limit, track your quota consumption across your models, and request further quota increases before usage is rate limited.
  • Cost: 
    InputTokenCount
    (uncached input), 
    CacheReadInputTokenCount
    , 
    CacheWriteInputTokenCount
    and 
    OutputTokenCount
    , each priced at its own rate. Cache reads cost less than uncached input, and cache writes can cost more depending on the model. A lower cache hit rate can increase cost per request.

On top of these metrics, we add cost per task. Our evals measure a score and a cost per task for every model and every reasoning effort we allow. Reasoning effort is a setting that controls how much a model reasons before it responds. We use the results to choose each default, which is the model and effort that our coding tools use unless an engineer picks another, and each effort ceiling, which is the highest effort we allow for a model.

Architecture

Engineers run AirChat on their AirDev workspaces, which are personal development machines in the cloud. They can also hand a task to AirChat Remote, which runs cloud agents in separate cloud workspaces while the engineer does something else. Both paths go through our LLM gateway to Amazon Bedrock.

Figure 1 shows how AirChat and AirChat Remote reach Amazon Bedrock through our gateway. It also shows how evals and production monitoring guide model defaults and effort ceilings.

The gateway records the model, client, team, and user for each request. We use these records only in aggregate, for cost and capacity planning. CloudWatch supplies token counts, latency, errors, and throttles. We compare those production signals with our eval scores and cost per task to decide when defaults or effort ceilings need to change.

Prerequisites

On the AWS side, you need:

  • Access to the models in Amazon Bedrock you plan to run and evaluate. For model availability by AWS Region, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.
  • Streaming calls through 
    ConverseStream
    or 
    InvokeModelWithResponseStream
    . Bedrock publishes 
    TimeToFirstToken
    only for the streaming APIs.
  • Model invocation logging, turned on in every AWS Region you call. It’s off by default. The logs can hold full prompts and responses along with the caller’s identity, so restrict who can read them and set a retention period.

Tagged IAM roles for your callers, with cost allocation tags activated. Activate them before you start collecting, because activation doesn’t backfill earlier costs.

You also need three things of your own:

  • A set of tasks from your own engineering work. Give each one a starting repository state, the prompt an engineer would write and a grader you trust. A grader is the program or model that scores the agent’s work. We build our tasks from real code changes, the review comments on those changes and the decisions that the original ticket didn’t spell out. Step 2 shows one.
  • A gateway or proxy in front of Bedrock that records the model, the client, the team, the user and the token counts for each request.
  • A table of public list prices for every model you run, with a date on each entry, so you can price eval tokens and production tokens on the same basis.

Before rollout, define what the agents can access and which actions need human review. Run code in isolated workspaces and test generated changes before merging. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can help filter harmful content and sensitive information in prompts and responses. For responses based on supplied reference material, contextual grounding checks can flag unsupported claims. Test these controls on your own tasks and include their latency and cost in your measurements.

Walkthrough

Start by measuring what a complete task costs. Then use those results to choose model defaults, check production behavior, manage capacity, and attribute spend.

Step 1: What does one finished task cost you?

A coding agent takes many requests to finish one task, and on each request the model re-reads the context so far. So we price the whole task.

Bedrock reports four kinds of tokens for each request: uncached input, cache reads, cache writes and output. In an eval run we price all four for every request and add up the requests in the task. Every cost in this post uses the public list prices dated for that run. We record the average cost next to the score for every model, reasoning effort and agent client we test, and the average includes low-scoring attempts.

Reasoning effort changes both score and cost. On one model we tested, moving from low to high effort raised the score by 0.8 points. Cost per task was 2.5 times as high. We use these results to set effort ceilings, which the gateway enforces.

Step 2: How fast can you evaluate a new model?

On the afternoon a new model came out, a single request to our agents started an eval campaign, which runs the new model through all our task suites. A suite is a fixed set of tasks of one type, and we have seven. Agents spread hundreds of tasks across the suites and several cloud workspaces, and each result appeared as soon as a grader scored it. First results arrived within hours. By the next morning, every suite had a score and a cost per task, and we had what we needed for a deployment decision for the entire org.

That speed depends on tasks that are already written down. Each task is a folder that holds everything one run needs. Here is a trimmed task from our machine learning work:

The grader recomputes the right answer from frozen data on every run, and the agent earns a reward of 1 only if every check passes. To test one model at every effort, list each effort as its own agent in a job config:

Both examples use the formats of Harbor, an open-source framework for running agent evals in sandboxes. It’s one option if you’re starting out.

Running the evals can be optimized. Writing the rubric, the scoring guide that a grader follows, is the hardest part. Our long tasks run over several rounds, with a simulated reviewer pushing back between rounds. A model grader scores each run on eight weighted dimensions. Each dimension gets a score from 0 to 3.

Because of ceilings like this one, an agent that needed rescuing can’t score well on polish alone.

Step 3: What do you watch after a rollout?

When latency rises, chart three signals before you open a support case: 

TimeToFirstToken
for the wait before generation starts, 
OutputTokenCount
for response length, and OTPS for generation speed. Bedrock has no native OTPS metric. You derive it with metric math, as the Amazon Bedrock User Guide describes:

In the example from our session, latency rose 40 percent while time to first token and OTPS stayed flat. Someone had changed the system prompt to ask for more thorough answers, and output tokens per request rose 50 percent. The model generated at the same speed and wrote longer responses. Treat prompt changes and model upgrades as deploys, and mark them on your dashboard.

Each week we put the CloudWatch runtime metrics next to the usage records from our gateway for each model. For cost and capacity planning, we also look at usage in aggregate: cost per request and the average number of requests per user each week. A new model can move both. After every rollout, we compare them with what we expected from the eval’s cost per task.

Step 4: The evals looked good. What did production show?

One model, which we call model A, looked good in our evals. On our coding tasks, it scored more than three points above our previous best model. Cost per task was about the same, and the same grader scored every model. We rolled it out, capped effort at high, and asked people to use low or medium for most work.

A few weeks after launch, we priced model A’s production usage at list price and looked at it in aggregate. Average weekly spend per user was several times higher on model A than on the model before it. Each model A request cost about three times as much, and the average model A user sent about three times as many requests.

Output tokens made up only a tenth of a request’s cost. Most of the cost went to cached context, which the model re-read on every request. Model A could work on its own for a long time, so people started long, self-directed sessions with it.

The eval measured the model on a task. Production measured how people chose to work with it.

Later, a newer model scored higher than model A on the same tasks and grader, at about a sixth of its cost per task. We moved model A’s users to it with a configuration change.

We then checked the change in aggregate on the same user group, the heavy users of model A. In their first full week on the newer model, the group sent about the same number of requests to their main model, and the group’s spend on that model fell to about a seventh.

Step 5: Why you get throttled, and where traffic goes next

On the 

bedrock-runtime
endpoint, Bedrock checks your tokens-per-minute quota when a request arrives, before the model writes anything. It reserves your uncached input tokens and your cache writes, plus 
max_tokens
, the most output the request is allowed. It adjusts that reservation as the model generates and returns the unused part when the request settles. Cache reads never count against the quota, so a request can be cheap against your quota and expensive on your bill. Output tokens settle at a burndown rate that is 1:1 on most models and several times that on some current models, so check your model’s rate.

A dashboard of billed tokens can show room while requests are being throttled. In our session’s example, the quota was 1 million tokens per minute and traffic was 300 requests per minute. The dashboard showed about 30 percent of quota. After applying a 5:1 output-token burndown rate, completed requests consumed about 77 percent.

Admission uses a different calculation. Each request initially reserved 600 uncached input tokens plus a 

max_tokens
of 4,096, for a total of 4,696 tokens. Responses were about 800 tokens at p99.

Lowering 

max_tokens
to 1,024 cut the initial reservation to 1,624 tokens, about 65 percent smaller. The limit was still above p99. For unchanged input and output, final quota consumption stays the same. The smaller reservation leaves more room to admit requests. Monitor 
stopReason
to catch truncated responses. Use backoff and jitter, and cap retries.

Demand can also outrun the headroom you have on any one model. You want to know where work can go before you need it, and our evals answer that. The answer can be a model from another model family. For every major model we use, we keep at least one equivalent that performs as well on our evals and that we can load-balance to. Without those evals, choosing where the work goes would be guesswork.

If headroom on a model stays tight, we can rebalance by changing a default in our configuration. First check that the equivalent model has capacity for the extra load and that your quota covers it. Keep enough traffic on it to hold your access, too: after a model enters its Legacy period, existing customers can lose access after 15 days of inactivity. A Legacy model works until end-of-life, and after that Bedrock removes it from every Region, requests to it fail, and Bedrock doesn’t move your traffic automatically. Alarm when 

LegacyModelInvocations
rises above zero.

Step 6: Whose spend is it?

Bedrock runtime metrics are dimensioned by 

ModelId
, so you can see which model served a request but not which team sent it. Bedrock publishes these metrics both with and without the 
ModelId
dimension, and a request that fails before Bedrock resolves the model appears only in the series without it, so filtering by 
ModelId
undercounts errors. Bedrock offers three ways to attribute spend:
  • Which team or user? Bedrock records the caller’s IAM identity on every request. Tag your roles, or pass session tags, to see cost by tag in AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0).
  • Which application? Application inference profiles are model-specific, so create one tagged profile per application and model, and call the matching profile’s ARN.
  • Which feature or prompt? Pass key-value pairs in 
    requestMetadata
    on 
    Converse
    . Bedrock writes them to the model invocation logs and leaves them off the bill. To price them, multiply the token counts in the logs by the published rates. Neither classic CUR nor CUR 2.0 carries a per-request ID, so reconcile the two by comparing totals by model, usage type and time period.

Behind a gateway, Bedrock sees the gateway’s role, so have the gateway assume a role for each user with its own 

RoleSessionName
or session tags. Cache those credentials for the session, because assuming a role on every request can exceed your AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) rate quotas. Requests keep succeeding when attribution breaks, so set an alarm for when Bedrock fails to deliver invocation logs.

Our usage records let us attribute usage by model, client, team and user, which we use only in aggregate for cost and capacity planning. We compute cost per task from the same four token counts, so we can compare token mix and cost between our evals and production.

Results

We can go from a model release to a deployment decision overnight. After one rollout, average weekly spend per user on model A was several times that on the previous model. We moved its heavy users to a newer model. In their first full week, the group’s spend on its main model fell to about a seventh, with roughly the same number of requests. For every major model we use, our evals identify an equivalent we can rebalance to.

Clean up

After testing, stop the eval jobs and agent processes you started. If you enabled model invocation logging only for this walkthrough, disable it in each Region using DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration.

After callers no longer use them, delete the application inference profiles you created using DeleteInferenceProfile. Remove IAM roles, policies, and resource tags created only for this walkthrough. Deactivate cost allocation tags used only for these tests. Delete test CloudWatch log groups and S3 log objects you no longer need.

Conclusion

We run four checks every time a model ships:

  • Release day: run the new model on your own tasks at every effort, and record a score and a cost per task together.
  • Before rollout: choose the default and cap effort from those numbers. Block any effort that costs more and scores less than a lower effort.
  • First weeks: compare cost per request and average requests per user with the eval’s cost per task, pricing both from the same four token counts.
  • Before you need it: know which models score the same on your evals, from any model family, and check their capacity and your quota before you rebalance.

We chose Amazon Bedrock for access to multiple model families through one API. It lets us use our existing AWS access controls and logging while AWS manages the model infrastructure. We use evals to choose models for our work and observability to know when those choices need another look.

To go further, see these pages in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide:

entries.title: Design responsible AI controls for Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL
entries.summary: Learn how to make RAG chatbot answers traceable with Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, pgvector, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, logging sources, scores, and guardrail traces in SQL.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Design responsible AI controls for Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL

A customer support chatbot that queries historical tickets and knowledge base articles stored in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition can deliver fast, context-aware answers. However, it also introduces challenges around privacy, accuracy, safety, and governance, especially when the underlying data contains sensitive customer information. In this post, we map the eight AWS Responsible AI (RAI) dimensions to Aurora PostgreSQL capabilities. We then walk through a design pattern for the Explainability dimension, using a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) based customer support chatbot as the reference use case. This post implements one dimension, Explainability, in depth. Treat it as Part 1 of a series rather than a full build-out of all eight.

Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition makes it more straightforward to operationalize responsible AI through its native Aurora Machine Learning (Aurora ML) capabilities. With Aurora ML, you can invoke Amazon SageMaker endpoints and Amazon Bedrock foundation models directly from SQL, without data movement, custom extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines, or complex integrations. This post uses Aurora ML to generate vector embeddings from SQL, keeping the embedding pipeline inside the database layer.

AWS defines eight core Responsible AI dimensions, published through the AWS Well-Architected Responsible AI Lens, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and the Responsible Use of AI Guide. These dimensions (Fairness, Explainability, Privacy and Security, Safety, Controllability, Veracity and Robustness, Governance, and Transparency) provide a structured framework for evaluating and implementing trustworthy AI systems.

Use case overview

Customer support systems often struggle to provide accurate, context-aware responses while maintaining privacy and compliance. Consider a customer support chatbot built on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL that uses RAG with pgvector embeddings, Amazon Bedrock model inference, and AWS Responsible AI guardrails to deliver grounded, explainable responses.

A customer can ask questions such as “Why was my last bill high?” or “Where is my last order?” and receive accurate answers with citations, while sensitive data remains obscured through personally identifiable information (PII) redaction and access controls.

Mapping the AWS Responsible AI dimensions to Aurora PostgreSQL

The following table maps the eight AWS Responsible AI dimensions to practical implementation strategies for a customer support chatbot built on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition. It highlights how database features, AWS AI services, and governance controls work together to deliver a trustworthy, secure, and explainable RAG-based chatbot.

RAI DimensionWhat It MeansImplementation ApproachesKey PostgreSQL / Aurora FeaturesPrimary AWS Services / Tools
1. FairnessChatbot should provide equal quality responses regardless of language, region, or customer profileBias testing using diverse support queries. Decouple demographics from embeddings. Metadata filtering and multilingual testing.pgvector, JSONB metadata, SQL filtering, viewsAmazon Bedrock Model Evaluation, Amazon SageMaker Clarify
2. ExplainabilityUsers and support teams should know why the chatbot gave a specific answerLog retrieved chunks, similarity scores, and citations. RAG tracing with source attribution. Full interaction logging.chat_interactions table, array columns, JSONB logs, pgvector similarityAmazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel
3. Privacy and SecurityProtect customer PII such as name, phone, and order details in ticketsPII redaction before embedding. Row-Level Security (RLS), encryption, IAM auth, RBAC, and anonymization.Row-Level Security, pgcrypto, roles, policiesAmazon Bedrock Guardrails, AWS KMS, Amazon Comprehend, AWS IAM
4. SafetyHelp prevent harmful, toxic, or inappropriate responsesContent filters, denied topics, prompt injection protection, rate limiting, and moderation.SQL functions, interaction logsAmazon Bedrock Guardrails
5. ControllabilityAbility to steer chatbot behavior and escalate to humansHuman-in-the-loop escalation, feedback table, feature flags, prompt control, and kill switch.chat_feedback table, escalation tables, triggersAmazon Bedrock Guardrails, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail
6. Veracity and RobustnessVerify accurate responses grounded in support data and avoid hallucinationsRAG grounding with similarity threshold. Versioned documents and validation checks.pgvector typed columns, CHECK constraints, triggersAmazon Bedrock Guardrails, Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation
7. GovernanceMaintain audit trail and accountability for chatbot decisionsAudit logging with retention policy. Model version tracking and Amazon S3 archival.pgaudit, pg_cron, JSONB model metadataAWS Audit Manager, AWS CloudTrail
8. TransparencyClearly inform users they are interacting with AI and show data sourcesPowered-by-AI notice, citations, privacy notice, and source explanation.SQL views, interaction logsAmazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, AWS AI Service Cards

Note: These are example approaches and may vary by use case.

Solution overview

This reference architecture shows how Responsible AI controls map to each component of a RAG-based chatbot on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition.

An ingestion pipeline redacts PII from support tickets, FAQs, and product documents, then converts them into vector embeddings. When a user submits a query, AWS Lambda runs a semantic search over Aurora PostgreSQL, applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for privacy and grounding, sends the guarded context to an Amazon Bedrock foundation model (FM), and logs every interaction for explainability and governance.

Lambda grounds responses in enterprise data, redacts PII and applies Row-Level Security (RLS) for privacy, records citations and interaction logs for explainability, and writes audit records for governance.

When to build this versus use a managed service: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides built-in RAG with citations and is the simpler choice when default retrieval and citation behavior meets your needs. Build the custom logging design in this post when you need provenance stored in your own schema. That provenance includes retrieved versus cited sources, similarity scores, and guardrail traces that you can query with SQL and retain under your own policies.

The following diagram illustrates the end-to-end architecture of this solution, showing the data ingestion flow (left), the query and response flow (center), and the responsible AI controls applied at each stage (center and right).

Data ingestion

An ingestion pipeline loads historical support tickets, FAQs, and product documentation into Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL after redacting PII, using the 

pgvector
and 
aws_ml
extensions for vector operations and Aurora ML integration.

The Aurora ML 

aws_bedrock.invoke_model_get_embeddings
function transforms the text into Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 vectors (1,024 dimensions), and 
pgvector
stores them.

Aurora PostgreSQL functions as both a relational store for structured customer data and a vector database for semantic search.

Query and response flow

When a user asks a question, the chatbot follows these steps (see Figure 1):

  • The user sends a natural language question to Amazon API Gateway over HTTPS.
  • API Gateway invokes AWS Lambda.
  • Turn the question into a vector. Lambda calls the Aurora ML 
    aws_bedrock.invoke_model_get_embeddings
    function with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2. This must be the same model used to embed the knowledge base, so the question and documents both produce comparable 1,024-dimension vectors.
  • Run a similarity search. Aurora PostgreSQL uses the 
    pgvector
    cosine distance operator to compare the question vector with the stored knowledge vectors, and returns the most relevant chunks with their similarity scores. Row-Level Security limits results to the current tenant.
  • Build the augmented prompt. Lambda combines the user’s question with the retrieved chunks, labeling each one 
    [Source N]
    . This gives the model knowledge from your database that it would not otherwise have.
  • Generate a grounded answer. Lambda sends the prompt to Amazon Bedrock. Guardrails check the input (content filters, denied topics, PII), the foundation model writes an answer based on the retrieved chunks, and a contextual grounding check confirms the answer is supported by those sources.
  • Log the interaction for explainability. Lambda writes the complete interaction to the 
    chat_interactions
    table: the question, retrieved chunk IDs, similarity scores, the sources actually cited, the guardrail trace, and the model ID.
  • Lambda returns the answer, with its source citations, to the user.

Supporting operations run separately from each request:

  • Ingestion: document embeddings are created once, when content is loaded (see Data ingestion).
  • Retention: 
    pg_cron
    archives older interaction records to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
  • Monitoring: Lambda sends logs and metrics to Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS CloudTrail records API activity for audit.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have the following in place:

  • An Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with the 
    pgvector
    extension enabled. HNSW indexes and iterative index scans require newer 
    pgvector
    versions, and Aurora ML and Amazon Bedrock model support are versioned separately. See the Aurora ML, pgvector, and Bedrock documentation for the current minimum versions rather than pinning to a specific one.
  • The 
    aws_ml
    extension enabled on the cluster (
    CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS aws_ml CASCADE
    ), with an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role attached to the cluster granting 
    bedrock:InvokeModel
    . Aurora ML calls Bedrock in the cluster’s own Region.
  • The 
    aws_s3
    extension enabled on the cluster (
    CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS aws_s3 CASCADE
    ), with an IAM role attached for the 
    s3Export
    feature so the retention job can export to Amazon S3.
  • Amazon Bedrock access with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 (
    amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0
    ) for embeddings and a foundation model that supports the Bedrock Converse API for answer generation. Model availability and recommended versions change over time, so choose a current model from Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. Newer models are invoked through cross-Region inference profile IDs.
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails configured for PII protection, content filtering, and contextual grounding (enable the contextual grounding policy in your Guardrail configuration).
  • IAM roles with appropriate permissions for Amazon Bedrock, Lambda, and Aurora PostgreSQL.
  • A custom cluster parameter group that adds 
    pgaudit
    and 
    pg_cron
    to the existing 
    shared_preload_libraries
    value (append to it rather than replacing it, so defaults such as 
    pg_stat_statements
    are preserved. This requires a cluster restart). Set 
    cron.database_name
    to your target database.
  • Basic familiarity with PostgreSQL, SQL, and Python.

Note: The prerequisites listed here focus on the database layer. Your application layer (for example, AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, and a chat UI) is separate and depends on your deployment architecture.

Design patterns for the Explainability dimension

This section presents the database-layer design patterns that make every AI-generated response traceable, from the user query, through retrieval and guardrail evaluation, to the final answer and its citations.

Step 1: Set up the database schema

Create the core tables for customer data, chat sessions, interaction logging, and feedback:

Start by creating the schema and the tables you need. Each table serves a specific Responsible AI dimension:

The customers table stores profiles for tenant-aware access control:

The chat_interactions table is the core of the Explainability implementation. It logs every query-response cycle with full RAG provenance, including retrieved chunk IDs, similarity scores, cited versus retrieved sources, guardrail traces, and the model used:

Because 

chat_interactions
stores raw 
request_text
and 
response_text
, protect it the same way as the source data: redact PII before the 
INSERT
(reusing the ingestion-time guardrail), or encrypt those columns with 
pgcrypto
, and apply Row-Level Security to the log tables so tenants cannot read each other’s interactions. Logging unprotected customer content would undercut the Privacy and Security control this design is meant to demonstrate.

The chat_feedback table captures user ratings and comments on chatbot responses, which supports the Controllability dimension. The 

ON DELETE CASCADE
clause makes sure the 90-day retention purge does not fail with foreign key violations:

Step 2: Prepare the knowledge base with pgvector and Aurora ML

Create the retrieval layer with vector embeddings, tenant isolation, and Aurora ML integration:

Create an HNSW index for fast approximate nearest neighbor search:

Enforce tenant isolation with Row-Level Security so that vector search results are scoped to the current tenant before data leaves the database:

Generate vector embeddings directly from SQL using Aurora ML, keeping the embedding pipeline inside the database layer:

Always redact PII before inserting data into the knowledge base. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (the 

ApplyGuardrail
API) or Amazon Comprehend (the 
detect_pii_entities
API) to identify and mask PII in your ingestion pipeline, as shown in the following example:

Step 3: Retrieve context and generate responses

When a query reaches your application layer, retrieve the top matching knowledge chunks using the 

pgvector
cosine similarity operator. The following SQL query shows this pattern:

Note: The 0.7 cosine-similarity cutoff drops weakly related chunks so the model is not grounded on noise. Tune it against your own data. The category filter and this threshold both post-filter HNSW results and may return fewer than 5 rows. Raise 

hnsw.ef_search
or use iterative index scans (
pgvector
0.8.0+) to compensate.

The following pseudocode shows the key patterns for contextual grounding, guardrail-intervention handling, citation parsing, and interaction logging. The snippets focus on the Responsible AI logic rather than application plumbing.

Use 

guardContent
blocks to enable contextual grounding in the Bedrock Converse API:

Check 

stopReason
to handle cases where the guardrail blocks the response:

Distinguish actually cited sources from all retrieved sources. On an Explainability post, this distinction is the point:

Log every interaction for Explainability. The 

INSERT
captures the full RAG provenance chain:

We define 

confidence_score
as the mean cosine similarity of the top-k retrieved chunks. The 
intent
field classifies the query (for example, 
billing
or 
order_status
), and 
response_latency_ms
records end-to-end inference time.

Step 4: Log interactions and add governance

Every chatbot interaction (the user query, retrieved chunks, similarity scores, response, and citations) is logged to the 

chat_interactions
table using the 
INSERT
shown in Step 3, supporting Explainability and Transparency. Customer feedback captured in 
chat_feedback
supports continuous improvement, reinforcing Controllability. For Governance, 
pgaudit
provides query audit trails, and 
pg_cron
drives automated data retention.

Set up 

pgaudit
and 
pg_cron
, which both require 
shared_preload_libraries
(see Prerequisites):

Query for governance review:

Archive both tables to Amazon S3 and purge only after the export succeeds. Running archive and purge as two independent cron jobs is unsafe: if the archive fails, a separately scheduled purge still deletes the rows. Wrap both in one function so the 

DELETE
runs only when the export returns. Also archive 
chat_feedback
, because the cascade would otherwise delete feedback that was not saved. The 90-day window matches a typical support-data retention policy. Adjust it to your own regulatory requirements.

Validate the solution

Run one question end to end, then read the row it produced. That single row is the evidence the design works: it shows which chunks were retrieved, how similar they were, which sources the answer actually cited, and the guardrail outcome.

Expected: One row whose 

cited_sources
is a subset of 
retrieved_chunk_ids
, 
similarity_scores
at or above your 0.7 threshold, and a 
guardrail_action
of 
NONE
for a clean question. If 
cited_sources
is empty, the model did not ground its answer and the response should be treated with caution.

Limitations and considerations

  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails adds latency to each inference call and incurs per-text-unit charges. Contextual grounding has additional pricing. Benchmark your response times and costs before production deployment.
  • Interaction logging grows storage over time. The S3 archival and purge cron jobs help manage this, but monitor your Aurora storage and adjust the retention period as needed.
  • HNSW indexes provide approximate nearest neighbor search. Post-filtering (for example, by category or tenant) runs after the index scan and may return fewer rows than your LIMIT. Increase 
    hnsw.ef_search
    or use iterative index scans (
    pgvector
    0.8.0+) to improve recall.
  • The contextual grounding check evaluates whether the model’s response is grounded in the provided context. It does not guarantee factual accuracy of the source documents themselves.
  • Aurora ML embedding generation runs synchronously in the database. For large batch ingestion, consider batching updates or using an asynchronous pipeline.
  • Everything in this post except Aurora ML (the 
    aws_bedrock.invoke_model_get_embeddings
