    calls) works on Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for PostgreSQL as well.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the following resources if you created them for this walkthrough:

  • Unschedule the cron job first, or it fails nightly once the schema is gone: 
    SELECT cron.unschedule('archive_and_purge');
    .
  • Drop the schema: 
    DROP SCHEMA rai_postgresql CASCADE;
    .
  • Delete the Amazon Bedrock Guardrail.
  • Remove the AWS Lambda functions and API Gateway endpoints.
  • Delete the Amazon S3 audit bucket (or configure a lifecycle policy).
  • Delete the Aurora PostgreSQL cluster (or stop it if you plan to reuse it).
  • Remove IAM roles created for Bedrock and Aurora ML integration.
  • Drop the application role (roles are not removed by 
    DROP SCHEMA
    ): 
    DROP ROLE app_user;
    .

Cost considerations: This solution uses Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Amazon Bedrock (model inference and embeddings), and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Costs vary by Region, instance size, request volume, and model choice. For pricing details, see the pricing pages for each service.

Conclusion

Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition, with 

pgvector
, Row-Level Security, 
pgaudit
, 
pgcrypto
, 
pg_cron
, and Aurora ML, provides database-layer building blocks for Responsible AI. Several dimensions also depend on AWS services outside the database, as the mapping table shows.

In this post, we focused on the Explainability dimension as a detailed design walkthrough. By logging retrieved chunk IDs, similarity scores, cited sources, and guardrail traces in Aurora, you get a queryable audit trail at the database layer. The mapping table shows how the remaining dimensions build on the same foundation, combining Aurora PostgreSQL features with AWS AI services.

The key takeaways from these design patterns are:

  • Log retrieval provenance at query time: retrieved and cited chunk IDs, similarity scores, and the guardrail trace.
  • Distinguish the sources actually cited from everything retrieved. That distinction is what makes an answer explainable.
  • Enforce tenant isolation with Row-Level Security, and set the tenant context before a vector search runs.
  • Archive audit data before purging, and protect the log tables as carefully as the source data.

As a next step, explore Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed RAG capability that now supports Aurora PostgreSQL as a vector store in many AWS Regions and provides built-in citation generation, which can help reduce the custom integration code required for Explainability in new projects.

entries.title: Private certificate authority support in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity
entries.summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now supports private certificate authorities (CAs), so your agents can connect to self-hosted identity providers that use a private CA. This post shows how to issue an IdP certificate with AWS Private CA, configure a credential provider to trust it, rotate the CA, and protect the certificate.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Private certificate authority support in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity

Many teams that build applications self-host their identity provider (IdP), such as Keycloak or PingFederate, inside a private network. These IdPs usually present a TLS server certificate from a private certificate authority (CA). With private CA support in AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, your agents can now connect to these IdPs while trusting the private CA that your organization already uses.

AgentCore Identity now supports private CA certificates for private identity providers. You store the PEM-encoded CA certificate in AWS Secrets Manager or Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference it from your credential provider. The CA certificate contains only the public certificate, not its private key. AgentCore Identity uses it to validate the server certificate presented by your IdP’s discovery, JSON Web Key Set (JWKS), and token endpoints. The CA certificate must be a root or intermediate CA certificate.

In this post, we show you how to issue an IdP certificate with AWS Private Certificate Authority. We then configure an AgentCore Identity credential provider to trust it and rotate the CA while minimizing downtime. We also show how to protect the CA certificate so that only your IdP team can change it. Although AgentCore Identity supports any private CA, including enterprise, third-party, and self-signed root CAs, the walkthrough in this post uses AWS Private CA and Keycloak as the IdP.

Solution overview

Consider an agent that needs to call an internal wiki API protected by your Keycloak IdP. The agent runs on AgentCore Runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which hosts your agent code. To get an OAuth 2.0 access token from Keycloak, the agent uses an AgentCore Identity credential provider, which holds the IdP connection details and client credentials.

The following diagram shows this setup. Keycloak runs in your virtual private cloud (VPC) behind an internal Application Load Balancer. The load balancer presents an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) private certificate signed by AWS Private CA. The CA certificate that AgentCore Identity trusts is stored in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3.

AgentCore Identity reaches the IdP privately through Amazon VPC Lattice, which connects to your VPC through a resource gateway, an entry point for VPC Lattice traffic into your VPC. VPC Lattice is required for private CA support. If you choose the managed option, AgentCore Identity creates and manages the VPC Lattice resources for you.

The flow works as follows:

  • You store the CA certificate in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3.
  • You create a credential provider that points to your IdP and to the CA certificate.
  • AgentCore Identity reads the CA certificate and checks that it’s a valid CA certificate.
  • Your agent requests an access token from AgentCore Identity.
  • AgentCore Identity connects to the IdP through VPC Lattice and checks the load balancer certificate against your CA.
  • The IdP issues the token and AgentCore Identity returns it to your agent.

Agents that use machine-to-machine, on-behalf-of, and user-delegated flows can also use the private CA without changing their code.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need:

  • An AWS account with access to the AgentCore console, in a supported AWS Region where AgentCore Identity supports private IdPs.
  • A self-hosted, OpenID Connect (OIDC) compliant IdP that runs in your VPC, with an OAuth client registered for your agent. The networking requirements, including subnets, security groups, and a private hosted zone for the IdP hostname, are described in Connect to private identity providers.
  • The latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and OpenSSL.
  • Permission to create credential providers, plus read access to the CA certificate. AgentCore Identity reads the certificate with the credentials of the principal that calls 
    CreateOauth2CredentialProvider
    , so that principal needs 
    secretsmanager:GetSecretValue
    on the secret or 
    s3:GetObject
    on the object. If the secret or object is encrypted with a customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key, the principal also needs 
    kms:Decrypt
    on that key.

Considerations

Keep the following in mind when you plan your deployment:

  • Private IdPs only: A credential provider or authorizer must have a 
    privateEndpoint
    to use a private CA. Otherwise, the request fails with the message 
    The private certificate authority feature can only be used with private IdP
    .
  • CA certificates in PEM format: The file must be PEM-encoded and no larger than 16 KB. It must contain only root or intermediate CA certificates that are within their validity period.
  • One certificate source per provider: Each credential provider references one secret or one S3 object. To trust more than one CA, put the certificates in the same PEM file.
  • Storage location: The secret or S3 object must be in the same AWS Region as the credential provider. Secrets Manager secrets must also be in the same account as the credential provider. S3 objects can be in another account when you provide 
    bucketOwnerAccountId
    and the bucket policy grants access.
  • Regions: Private CA support depends on VPC Lattice and is available in the AWS Regions where AgentCore Identity supports private IdPs.

Walkthrough

The walkthrough has four steps. If your IdP already presents a certificate from your enterprise CA, skip to Step 2.

Step 1: Issue a server certificate for your IdP

Start by creating a root CA in AWS Private CA. For instructions, see Create a private CA and Install the CA certificate. Choose general-purpose mode, because short-lived certificate mode issues certificates that are valid for 7 days or less. When you create the CA, authorize ACM to renew certificates, so that ACM can renew the IdP’s server certificate before it expires.

Next, request the server certificate. AgentCore Identity checks that the certificate matches the IdP hostname, so include each hostname that appears in your IdP’s discovery document as a subject alternative name (SAN). In most Keycloak deployments, the discovery, JWKS, and token endpoints share one hostname. For example, if your discovery URL is 

https://keycloak.example.local/realms/agents/.well-known/openid-configuration
, add 
keycloak.example.local
as a SAN.

To request a private certificate for the IdP (console)

  • Open the ACM console and choose Request.
  • Choose Request a private certificate and then choose Next.
  • For Certificate authority, choose the CA that you created.
  • For Fully qualified domain name, enter the IdP hostname, for example 
    keycloak.example.local
    .
  • Choose Request.
  • Attach the certificate to the HTTPS listener of the internal load balancer in front of your IdP. For instructions, see Update an HTTPS listener.

Step 2: Store the CA certificate

AgentCore Identity needs to trust the CA certificate to validate the IdP’s server certificate. Because it trusts the CA rather than the server certificate itself, you don’t need to update the credential provider each time the server certificate renews.

Export the CA certificate from AWS Private CA in PEM format:

Before you upload the file, check it against the requirements. The file must be PEM-encoded and meet size requirements, containing only CA certificates that are within their validity period. The following commands show the CA flag, expiry date, and file size. The last command confirms that the IdP’s certificate chains to this CA. Run it from a host that can reach the IdP. It returns Verify return code: 0 (ok) when the chain is valid.

The output looks similar to the following:

Store the file in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3. A Secrets Manager secret must be a string secret in the same account as the credential provider. An S3 object can be in another account, which suits organizations that run the IdP in a central account.

Give write access to the secret or object only to the team that operates your IdP. For an example policy, see Protect the CA certificate later in this post.

Step 3: Create the credential provider

You can create the credential provider in the AgentCore console or with the AWS CLI. The private CA settings appear on the console only after you connect the OAuth client to a VPC, because private CA support applies only to private IdPs.

To create a credential provider that trusts your private CA (console)

  • Open the AgentCore console and in the navigation pane under Connections, choose Outbound Auth. Then choose Add OAuth client.
  • For Provider, choose Customized provider. For Configuration type, choose Discovery URL and enter your IdP’s discovery URL, for example 
    https://keycloak.example.local/realms/agents/.well-known/openid-configuration
    . Then enter the client ID and client secret.
  • Expand Additional configurations. Under VPC security, choose Managed and select the VPC, subnets, and security groups that can reach the IdP. If you manage your own VPC Lattice resources, choose Self-managed and select the resource configuration instead.
  • Under Root certificate authority, choose Add root certificate.
  • In the Add root certificate panel, for Certificate source, choose AWS Secrets Manager and select the secret that you created in Step 2. To use Amazon S3, choose Amazon S3 and enter the S3 URI. For an object in another account, also enter the Bucket owner account ID.
  • Choose Apply.
  • Choose Add OAuth client.

The Root certificate authority field accepts either a root or an intermediate CA certificate.

To create the same credential provider with the AWS CLI, add certificateConfigurations to the custom OAuth 2.0 provider configuration:

To use Amazon S3 instead, replace the 

certificateConfigurations
entry with 
{"s3": {"uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/trust-anchors/keycloak-root-ca.pem", "bucketOwnerAccountId": "444455556666"}}
. If you leave out bucketOwnerAccountId, AgentCore Identity expects the bucket to be in your own account. To keep the client secret out of your shell history, you can reference a client secret that you store in Secrets Manager.

Step 4: Verify the credential provider

AgentCore Identity validates the certificate and sets up private connectivity in the background, so a new credential provider starts in the 

CREATING
status. Check the status after a few minutes:

On the console, the credential provider’s details page shows the configured certificate under Root certificates. When the status is READY, your agents can request tokens from the IdP. If the status is 

CREATE_FAILED
, the 
failureReason
field explains why. For example, 
Leaf certificates are not allowed, must provide CA certificates only
means that you uploaded the server certificate instead of the CA certificate. If you see 
Unable to access S3 object
or 
Secrets Manager can't find the specified secret
, check that the URI or Amazon Resource Name (ARN) is correct. Also confirm that your identity can read the object or secret. If the provider is 
READY
but token requests fail, confirm that the IdP’s server certificate was issued by the configured CA and has a SAN that matches the IdP hostname.

Monitor and rotate the CA certificate

After you verify that the credential provider trusts the private CA, monitor the CA certificate’s expiration and rotate it before it expires to prevent token request failures. AgentCore Identity publishes the 

EarliestCertificateDaysToExpiry
metric to Amazon CloudWatch in the 
AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore
namespace when your agents request tokens through a credential provider that uses a private CA. The metric reports the days remaining until the earliest certificate in your PEM file expires. It has 
ProviderName
, 
ProviderArn
, and 
TokenVault
dimensions. When you create an alarm, specify all three. We recommend a CloudWatch alarm that notifies you well before the value reaches zero, because token requests to the IdP stop working when the CA certificate expires.

NOTE: AgentCore Identity reads the certificate only when you create or update the credential provider. If you change the secret or S3 object, call 

UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider
afterward so that AgentCore Identity reads the new content. Include 
certificateConfigurations
in the update request. If you leave it out, the credential provider stops trusting your private CA.

A PEM file can contain more than one CA certificate and AgentCore Identity trusts each of them. You can use this to rotate to a new CA while minimizing downtime:

  • Combine the current and new CA certificates in one file, for example with 
    cat current-ca.pem new-ca.pem > rotation.pem
    . Upload the file to your secret or S3 object.
  • Call 
    UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider
    and wait for the status to return to 
    READY
    .
  • Replace the IdP’s server certificate with one issued by the new CA.
  • After token requests succeed, upload a file that contains only the new CA certificate and call 
    UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider
    again.

AgentCore Identity doesn’t check certificate revocation lists (CRLs) or use the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP). This means that if an unauthorized party obtains the private key for an IdP server certificate, AgentCore Identity continues to trust that certificate. This trust lasts until the certificate expires or until you stop trusting the CA that issued it. To stop trusting a CA, remove it from the PEM file and update the credential provider.

Protect the CA certificate

A CA certificate contains no private key and is public by design, because you hand it to every client that has to trust your IdP. What you need to protect is the data integrity of the trust store, meaning the secret or S3 object that holds the certificate. If someone replaces the certificate or adds another CA certificate to the trust store, the next update could let an unauthorized party who can redirect traffic impersonate your IdP.

We recommend that you scope permissions around writes rather than reads. Give write access, such as 

s3:PutObject
or 
secretsmanager:PutSecretValue
, only to the team or pipeline that operates the IdP. Give read access to the principals that call 
CreateOauth2CredentialProvider
or 
UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider
. During these operations, AgentCore Identity reads the CA certificate using the caller’s IAM permissions. The following bucket policy for a central identity account (444455556666) lets only the role that manages credential providers in a workload account (111122223333) read the CA certificates. It also requires that role to belong to your organization in AWS Organizations, and it denies writes from principals other than the IdP administrator role:

The principal in the workload account also needs 

s3:GetObject
in its own IAM policy. For Secrets Manager, which must be in the same account, use a resource-based policy on the secret to restrict writes to the IdP administrator role.

Because the secret is in the same account, IAM policies can grant read access, so the resource policy only needs to deny changes:

Turn on S3 Versioning to recover an overwritten file and AWS CloudTrail data events to record each change. Because the CA certificate isn’t confidential, SSE-S3 encryption is sufficient and avoids the cross-account AWS KMS permissions that a customer managed key requires.

Keep the trust scope of each credential provider narrow. Upload only the CA that issues your IdP’s server certificate, rather than your organization’s full trust bundle. If your IdPs use different CAs, store each CA certificate in its own secret or S3 object so that each credential provider trusts only the CA that it needs.

Use a private CA for inbound authorization

You can also use a private CA for inbound authorization. When AgentCore Runtime or AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) issued by a private IdP, it fetches the IdP’s discovery document and its signing keys from the JWKS endpoint. AgentCore Gateway validates the discovery URL when you create the gateway. If the CA certificate is missing or doesn’t match the IdP’s certificate chain, the gateway status changes to 

FAILED
with the reason 
Failed to validate discovery url
. To trust a private CA for that connection, add 
certificateConfigurations
to the 
customJWTAuthorizer
configuration, next to the existing 
privateEndpoint
:

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources that you created:

  • Delete the credential provider in the AgentCore console, or run 
    aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-oauth2-credential-provider --name keycloak-private-ca
    .
  • Delete the secret in Secrets Manager or the object in Amazon S3.
  • Remove the certificate from the load balancer listener and then delete it in ACM.
  • Disable and then delete the private CA in the AWS Private CA console. AWS Private CA charges a monthly fee for each CA until you delete it. For details, see AWS Private CA pricing.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to connect AgentCore Identity to a self-hosted IdP that uses a certificate from your own CA. You issued a server certificate with AWS Private CA, stored the CA certificate in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3 and referenced it from a credential provider. You also saw how to rotate the CA with a combined PEM file and how to limit who can change the certificate that your agents trust.

To learn more, see Connect to private identity providers in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. For examples using Keycloak, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment on this post.

entries.title: How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
entries.summary: Learn how Salesforce uses the cross-Region inference router in Amazon SageMaker AI to turn fragmented Regional capacity into reliable model serving. Salesforce adds capacity securely across Regions and accounts while keeping its data residency commitments, and sees per request where each call was served and why.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

Thanks to Amit Gupta, Senior Director- AI/ML and Mark Wang, Software Engineering PMTS from Salesforce for your contributions in the vision and partnership of cross-Region inference routing on SageMaker AI.

Salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves a wide variety of models for products across Salesforce, including Agentforce and the Salesforce Trust Layer, in 30+ global Regions. These include both models trained in house and open source models. Hosting models separately in each Region splits capacity and makes traffic spikes harder to absorb, which turns a capacity shortfall into an availability problem.

This post shows how Salesforce set up the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI and how it lets the team add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments. It also walks through how Salesforce sees where each request was served and why. The cross-Region inference routing gives an application one invocation path across SageMaker AI endpoints in several Regions and accounts, and sends each request to an endpoint that can serve it. Those endpoints are Salesforce’s own, already deployed. The post starts with the capacity problem Salesforce faced, explains how the router works and how Salesforce integrated it into its Internal Gateway, walks through an example setup, and then describes what the team observed.

Why serving these models makes capacity a reliability problem

Salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves customers from the Region their requests come from, across 30+ global Regions and hundreds of AWS accounts, and they provision capacity based on each customer’s traffic. Every customer has its own peak window, and those windows often overlap. Provisioning for the overlapping peak would be the safe choice, but it costs too much. Customers also onboard new business units at short notice, so they must grow the fleet quickly. Adding capacity quickly, Region by Region, leaves Salesforce with capacity fragmentation: some Regions have idle instances while others run out.

Before the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI, Salesforce used its Internal Gateway to send traffic that the local endpoints couldn’t handle to other Regions. The team built and operated this path, supported by basic health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic. That approach had two gaps. First, the gateway had no capacity signals from either the local or the remote endpoint, so it couldn’t tell when to shift traffic or whether the destination had room. Second, cross-Region traffic had to leave the virtual private cloud (VPC) through a NAT gateway and an internet gateway and travel over public AWS networking. In design reviews, the team also raised the risk of cascading failures: moving traffic during an incident can overload the next Region, so Salesforce needed a cap on cross-Region traffic.

Building this logic separately in every application doesn’t scale across Salesforce. The team needed a managed, capacity-aware routing path.

What the inference router does

The inference router is a Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account. Your application invokes the router instead of an endpoint, passing a routing target name with the same request body and content type it sends to 

InvokeEndpoint
today. A routing target is a name you choose for one logical model, such as a toxicity classifier, and it lists the endpoints and inference components that may serve that model by their full Amazon Resource Names (ARNs). A router holds one routing target per model, and a problem with one model’s endpoints does not move traffic for the others. A routing target can mix single-model endpoints and inference components.

Because each destination is named by its ARN, it can be in another Region or another AWS account. The account that owns an endpoint grants access through a resource-based endpoint policy that allows one named router to invoke it, which is how Salesforce runs it.

The router prefers its own Region, and while the local destination serves successfully, requests stay there. The router judges each destination by the outcomes of recent requests. Platform faults, 5xx errors from the model container, throttles, and timeouts lower a destination’s health. As they persist, the router moves a growing share of new requests to healthy destinations, typically starting within about a minute. It can take several minutes for a destination with little traffic. Signals such as scaling progress and failed instance launches affect how quickly the router responds once errors appear, but they do not move traffic by themselves. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left, so it does not swing back and forth. When a destination fails a request without running the model, for example by throttling it, the router retries that request once on another destination.

Client errors such as invalid input do not move traffic, because they would fail the same way in any Region. Model latency does not move traffic either, because a slow response often reflects a long prompt or output and does not by itself mean the endpoint is unhealthy. The router also does not deploy models, copy artifacts, or add instances. It uses the capacity you have deployed, and each endpoint’s own autoscaling keeps adding instances as its traffic grows.

How Salesforce integrated the router into its Internal Gateway

In Salesforce’s Internal Gateway, the router call sits exactly where the direct 

InvokeEndpoint
call used to be: in the per-request egress path, after the data residency check and before response handling. That check is the one routing decision the gateway keeps. A request tagged with a residency requirement is pinned to its in-Region routing target, whose only destination is the local endpoint, so it can never fail over across a boundary. Everything else goes to the router with the same body, content type, and accept type the gateway already sent. Capacity awareness, health assessment, and failover now live in the routing layer instead of in Salesforce’s code.

Salesforce treats the two routing fields on every response as first-class telemetry. The gateway logs InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason on the same structured line as the existing request ID and trace ID, and emits them as application performance monitoring (APM) tags. Because the ARN carries the Region and account, a single log line shows whether a request ran locally or crossed a boundary, and why: local-preferred, failover, capacity-available, or only-healthy. The team joins these fields against the router’s Amazon CloudWatch metrics when investigating a traffic shift.

The gateway’s timeout accounts for cross-Region round-trip latency, so a request that fails over has time to complete in the remote Region. Because the router already retries once on another destination, the gateway adds no retries of its own, which keeps attempts from multiplying during an incident.

Example setup

The following walkthrough shows the configuration Salesforce tested, using example IDs and names. Salesforce first created a router in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) with a local destination and confirmed that requests were routed to it. The team then registered an endpoint in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2) owned by a different account, removed the local destination, and confirmed that requests reached the remote endpoint across the account and Region boundary. In the examples, the router account is 111122223333, and the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint is 444455556666.

Authorize the router on the destination endpoint

In the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, with a condition that limits access to one named router. The router does not need to exist yet, so you can use the ARN of the router you plan to create.

The 

sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn
condition means the router account can reach the endpoint only through that router. The endpoint owner can revoke access at any time with 
delete-endpoint-policy
.

Create the router

In the router account, create the router in us-west-2 with one routing target that lists both destinations by ARN.

Each additional model becomes another entry in 

RoutingTargets
.

Confirm that each destination is routable

Before sending traffic, call 

DescribeInferenceRouter
and check each destination’s 
RoutingStatus
. Routable means SageMaker AI could read the destination and it can serve traffic. Unroutable means the destination was read but can’t serve right now, for example because the endpoint is not InService. Unknown means SageMaker AI couldn’t read the destination with your credentials, for example because you lack 
sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint
(or 
sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent
for an inference component), or, for a destination in another account, because its endpoint policy doesn’t grant Describe.

Invoke the router instead of the endpoint

The change in the calling code is small. The request body, content type, and accept type stay exactly as they were. The client and operation change, and the endpoint name is replaced by the router name and the routing target name.

An 

InferenceId
and 
CustomAttributes
are passed through to the destination as with 
InvokeEndpoint
, so identifiers such as a trace ID travel with the request. Members such as 
TargetVariant
and 
InferenceComponentName
are not used, because the routing target replaces them.

Seeing where requests went

Most teams evaluating a routing layer first ask how to tell what it did. The inference router answers on every response and in Amazon CloudWatch. Each response carries the ARN of the destination that served it and a routing reason, in the InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason fields and in the matching X-Amzn-SageMaker-Invoked-Routed-Resource-Arn and X-Amzn-SageMaker-Invoked-Routing-Reason headers. Because the ARN includes the Region and account, logging both values with your own request logs gives you a per-request record of whether each call ran locally or crossed a boundary.

The routing reason takes one of four values. 

local-preferred
means a healthy destination in the router’s Region served the request. 
failover
means a destination in the router’s Region exists but isn’t serving reliably, so the router sent the request elsewhere. 
capacity-available
means no destination in the router’s Region could take the request, and it went to one of several healthy destinations in other Regions. 
only-healthy
means it was served by the only eligible destination that was healthy.

In aggregate, the router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, each carrying the router name and destination ARN, so the cross-Region picture is visible from one place. 

aws.sagemaker.inference_router.invocations
counts requests per destination, and its 
error.type
attribute splits failures into invocation_4xx, invocation_5xx (including timeouts), and invocation_model_error for errors returned by the model.

aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.duration
measures the time each destination took, and 
aws.sagemaker.inference_router.overhead.duration
measures the time the router added, including the network to and from a remote Region. 
aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.status
reports each destination’s health state as 
healthy
, 
overloaded
, or 
degraded
. You query these metrics with PromQL in CloudWatch Query Studio, and you can place them next to each endpoint’s existing SageMaker AI metrics on a cross-account, cross-Region dashboard.

Testing failover across accounts and Regions

Salesforce tested the router in two configurations. First, same-Region routing in us-west-2, where the Internal Gateway called the local inference router and the router sent requests to the local Endpoint A. Second, cross-account, cross-Region routing, where the router in us-west-2 also listed an endpoint in us-east-2 owned by a separate infrastructure account. Before sending traffic, the team called 

DescribeInferenceRouter
and confirmed that the routing target listed both destinations and that both reported a 
RoutingStatus
of Routable. Requests sent to the router were then served by the local endpoint, with a routing reason of local-preferred. Setup took little effort: the endpoint owner added an endpoint policy for the router’s account, and the router call replaced the direct 
InvokeEndpoint
call in the gateway’s egress path, with the same request body, content type, and accept type.

To test failover, the team flooded the local endpoint in us-west-2 until it was saturated, while a separate probe kept invoking the router and recorded where each request was served and how long it took. For about five minutes of saturation, probe latency at p50 rose from 0.2 seconds to 45 to 58 seconds, and traffic stayed in us-west-2. This is the intended behavior, because latency alone does not move traffic. When requests began to exceed the model container’s 60-second handler timeout and return errors, the router started to shift traffic. The first requests reached us-east-2 about two minutes after the first errors, and within another minute about 78 percent of probe traffic was served in us-east-2. The remaining 20 to 25 percent stayed local so the router could detect recovery.

Once traffic had moved, p50 latency returned to 0.2 seconds, and the cross-Region path added under 100 milliseconds at p50. After the local endpoint recovered, traffic returned to us-west-2 gradually over about 10 minutes, and the probe recorded no errors during failover or failback. The InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason fields on each response, together with the router’s per-destination invocation metrics in CloudWatch, showed the whole sequence without any extra instrumentation.

The router lets Salesforce replace operational logic the team used to build and run itself: the health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic in the Internal Gateway. Capacity signals and failover now live in the routing layer, not in each application.

Before broader adoption, Salesforce plans to repeat the failover test with the local endpoint held at saturation for longer, measure cross-Region latency at millisecond precision, evaluate cascading-Region behavior at the cross-Region cap, and roll out the router across more Regions.

“With the new cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI, we can add capacity securely and keep our data residency commitments. Workloads that must stay in a region stay there, and only eligible traffic can be served from another Region. A single managed call works alongside our existing failover logic, so we didn’t have to re-architect our application or change our payloads. SageMaker AI handles routing, health detection, and fallback, and customer data always stays within the Salesforce trust boundary. We decide which Regions are eligible and control access through endpoint policies that we own. Because inference router works with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail, we also get a complete observability, cost-tracking, and governance architecture for our workloads.”

— Richard Chang, Software Engineering Architect, Salesforce

Best practices and what to watch

Keep the same model, container image, and artifacts available in every Region you register, because the router does not copy them, and a destination that runs a different model version will return different answers to the same request.

Size each destination Region for its own traffic plus the overflow you expect to send it. The router does not create capacity, and if every eligible destination is busy, your application receives the destinations’ own errors. Configure autoscaling on each destination the way you do today, with enough headroom that a receiving endpoint can scale out under its own policy when traffic arrives from another Region.

Customers can set the cap in the receiving endpoint’s configuration (

CrossRegionTrafficConfig
), as a per-instance request rate and the largest share of the endpoint’s capacity that remote traffic may use. Local traffic never counts against the cap. When remote traffic reaches it, the endpoint stops accepting additional requests from other Regions and the router sends them to other destinations, so local callers keep their capacity. The cap applies to real-time endpoints.

Conclusion

Salesforce serves a wide variety of models for products across the company in 30+ global Regions, and hosting them separately in each Region had turned capacity shortfalls into availability problems. With the inference router, Salesforce registers the endpoints it already runs in different Regions and accounts behind one call, so traffic that a local endpoint cannot serve reaches capacity elsewhere instead of failing. Requests that must stay in a Region stay there, endpoint owners authorize cross-account access through policies they control, and every response shows where a request ran and why. SageMaker AI handles the routing, health assessment, and gradual return of traffic after recovery, instead of each calling application building that logic itself. This lets Salesforce add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments.

The cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI is generally available starting November 18, 2026, in all commercial Regions where inference is supported for real-time endpoints. To get started, see the Inference router documentation in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide and the CreateInferenceRouter API reference.

entries.title: How Social Department built culture-aware video discovery
entries.summary: Social Department, an AI operating system for entertainment marketing, worked with TrackIt and AWS to build QuickSearch: single-action queries that surface shareable scenes, quotable lines, memeable frames, and trend-aligned moments across large video libraries, using TwelveLabs models on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Social Department built culture-aware video discovery

This post is co-written by Mariah Miller and Sirajus Salekin from AWS and Nicholas Chase from Social Department.

Entertainment marketing teams manage tens of thousands of video assets across studios, networks, and streaming applications. Most campaigns begin with the same video discovery problem: finding the one moment in the footage that will resonate with an audience. When a brief lands, the clock starts, and what they need is almost never something a database can describe.

Semantic search, on its own, has a ceiling: It answers the question you can articulate. Ask it for a character holding a coffee mug and it will find every coffee mug in a thousand episodes. The queries that actually drive entertainment campaigns look nothing like that. They are questions of judgment: which moment in a show will travel, which line is quotable, and which single frame will work as a meme.

Those questions can’t be typed into a search box. Answering them requires two things the search index doesn’t have: an editorial definition of what “quotable” or “memeable” means for a given library, and a continuously refreshed view of what is moving outside the library. Historically, answering them meant a person with deep knowledge of the show watching footage for a week, and that person doesn’t scale across a catalog.

In this post, we describe how Social Department, the AI operating system for entertainment marketing, set out to encode those editorial questions as executable retrieval pipelines. The result is QuickSearch, a set of single-action queries that return the clips a marketer is looking for without requiring them to describe it: Shareable Scenes, Quotable Quotes, Memeable Moments, and Trend Align.

The models in this solution run on Amazon Bedrock, so customer data stays within the AWS data boundary. It isn’t shared with model providers and isn’t used to train the underlying models.

Social Department’s approach to responsible AI is that AI proposes and people decide. In production, code checks generated output against the source material (for example, a quote is discarded if it isn’t in the episode transcript). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails helps screen customer search text for prompt attacks, and a person on the customer’s team approves every post before it publishes.

Social Department owns the pipeline architecture, the retrieval system, and the editorial criteria behind each action. TrackIt, an AWS Premier Tier Services Partner, implemented and delivered against that design. TwelveLabs’ Marengo 3.0 and Pegasus 1.2 models on Amazon Bedrock provide the scene-level video reasoning the pipeline builds on. AWS supplies the infrastructure, the model access including Anthropic’s Claude models, and Amazon OpenSearch Service, using its serverless option, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, for retrieval.

A note on scope: This post describes the AWS portions of the system: the ingest and indexing pipeline, the retrieval path, and the services that run them. The components Social Department owns, including its media and data backbone, content analysis and discovery engine, editorial criteria, and evaluation program, are described only to the depth needed to follow the architecture. The named services that follow are the ones this post is about, not an inventory of Social Department’s full system.

About Social Department

Social Department is the AI operating system for entertainment marketing, serving major studios, networks, streamers, and FAST applications. It automates campaign strategy, asset creation, publishing, and performance optimization across a client’s full content library. Most of those functions depend on locating the right moment inside the footage first, and semantic clip discovery has been core to the product from the beginning.

Why semantic search alone was insufficient

Entertainment marketing operates under two constraints that a general-purpose search layer can’t satisfy.

The valuable queries are the ones nobody can phrase

A marketer can describe an object, a location, or a line of dialogue, but not what will travel. That judgment, this moment lands and that one doesn’t, is the actual skill in the job. It was never automatable because it depends on knowing how an audience behaves rather than what a video contains. A search layer that only understands content requires a human to supply the intent, and supplying that intent well requires having already watched the show.

Trend signal lives outside the library and moves on a different clock

No amount of video understanding tells you what audiences are talking about this morning. That information is created outside the library and changes hourly, while a library changes only when new content is added. A system that answers these queries has to acquire trend signal continuously and reconcile it against the library at request time.

That distinction drove the core architectural decision: content understanding and trend acquisition run as independent pipelines on their own schedules and are joined only when a user selects a QuickSearch action.

Solution overview

With QuickSearch, teams can interact with a video library in a different way, one where the system proposes rather than waits. It provides four actions, each with its own retrieval strategy, editorial criteria, and ranking model. The walkthrough that follows describes how each is implemented. The list here introduces what they do.

  • Shareable Scenes surfaces substantial, self-contained scenes such as extended confrontations, climaxes, and set pieces, biased toward developed sequences rather than quick reactions.
  • Quotable Quotes finds punchy, quotable dialogue capped at short clip lengths, weighting up lines that have demonstrably circulated where that signal is available for the title.
  • Memeable Moments identifies individual frames that will function as memes and generates a caption grounded in the actual frame. A dedicated extraction and scoring step chooses the frame rather than taking a thumbnail.
  • Trend Align takes what is trending right now and finds the moments in the library that legitimately connect to it, so a title that finished airing years ago can re-enter a live conversation.

Alongside these, Social Department keeps natural-language search for everything the actions don’t cover, and image-based search, where a reference image returns visually similar content across the library.

The following diagram shows how the three parts of the architecture connect. The content understanding pipeline makes the library searchable, and the trend acquisition lanes pull in external trend signal. The QuickSearch job layer joins the two at request time.

Architecture walkthrough

The system has three parts that run on independent schedules. Two acquire and structure information. The third resolves a user’s single selection into a multi-stage retrieval operation across both.

Content understanding pipeline

This pipeline makes the library legible. It works asynchronously on ingest. An AWS Step Functions state machine orchestrates roughly two dozen Python AWS Lambda functions end to end. The following steps trace one video from upload to indexed clips.

  • Upload and trigger – Video lands in a per-team Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket. The S3 Object Created event, routed through Amazon EventBridge, starts the Step Functions execution.
  • Metadata – The first Lambda function resolves title, team, episode, and public identifiers against Social Department’s media and data backbone, writes video metadata to Amazon DynamoDB, and reports the asset as processing.
  • Transcode – AWS Elemental MediaConvert transcodes the asset to 480p H.264 with adaptive deinterlacing, using a Step Functions task token so the state machine waits on the job rather than polling.
  • Shot detection – Amazon Rekognition performs asynchronous segment detection with an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) callback. A second Lambda function merges and splits the raw shots into content-aware ranges of roughly 10–20 seconds. Those ranges are the unit the rest of the pipeline fans out over. Within a range, Social Department segments embeddings at a fixed interval, a design choice tuned to the pacing of episodic television. The indexed clip is short and fixed-length, but the range it sits in follows the cut.
  • Embedding – Ranges are processed in a Step Functions Distributed Map. Each call passes a start and end time to TwelveLabs Marengo 3.0 on Amazon Bedrock through asynchronous invocation. The call produces multimodal embeddings across visual, audio, and transcript dimensions, with no file splitting needed on this path.
  • Scene description – TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.2 on Amazon Bedrock runs per segment in a parallel Distributed Map, producing scene-level narrative descriptions, emotions, themes, dialogue type, and narrative position, which form the text layer the ranking models later reason over. Pegasus takes pre-cut files rather than time ranges, so a separate Lambda function cuts each range first, with a few seconds of padding on either side to preserve scene transitions.
  • Transcription and enrichment – In parallel with embedding, the pipeline runs speech-to-text with automatic fallback, and Amazon Rekognition for on-screen text, visual labels, and face collections used in character grounding. Anthropic’s Claude models on Amazon Bedrock extract the show’s character map and generate show-level concepts and character roles.
  • Indexing – Amazon Bedrock writes embedding output to Amazon S3. A final Distributed Map then indexes embeddings, transcript, on-screen text, scene description fields, and labels into Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.

The pipeline is event-driven end to end. Every Lambda task retries with exponential backoff. The scene-description stage adds a dedicated throttling retry with full jitter. Non-critical enrichment steps degrade gracefully rather than failing the run, and a hard failure routes to an error handler that records the reason and reports the asset as failed.

Same-Region staging for Marengo. Marengo is available in a specific set of AWS Regions. Asynchronous invocation in Amazon Bedrock reads input from and writes output to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region as the endpoint. The pipeline is built around those parameters. It stages each video into a dedicated bucket in US East (N. Virginia) before invoking Marengo, then reads the embedding output back from the same bucket. The rest of the infrastructure stays in its home Region while each embedding job runs alongside the model. For model availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

Trend acquisition

This pipeline operates continuously and independently of any library, and it is what makes Trend Align possible.

  • Two lanes, one feed – Trend data is acquired through two lanes with deliberately different mechanisms. The daily lane uses an Amazon EventBridge cron, one scheduled fetch per region per day, timed to each region’s local morning rather than a fixed UTC hour. The heat lane (Heat Seeker) reads early-stage, momentum-ordered trends, and is fetched only when a user explicitly asks for it, reusing what is already stored if it is recent enough. The split is a cost decision. A cron pays for every region on every tick whether or not anyone is working, while a demand-shaped fetch behind a TTL costs nothing on a quiet day.
  • Regional feeds are separate populations – Trends are acquired per geographic region, currently four feeds: worldwide, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia. A region isn’t a filter over a global list. Each is discovered separately on its own schedule, so the same day’s trends genuinely differ between them.
  • Interpretation and the editorial gate – Raw trend data isn’t shown to a customer. Anthropic’s Claude Haiku on Amazon Bedrock normalizes each trend onto Social Department’s own category schema, standardizes its description, deduplicates near-matches, and caps how many survive per category. In the same pass, an editorial gate drops trends whose primary subject is death, violence, self-harm, natural disaster, politics, protest, crime, or a public-health crisis. A marketing customer isn’t offered these, regardless of how large the trend is. Rejected trends are remembered so each fetch doesn’t re-screen them.
  • Storage as first-class rows – Interpreted trends are upserted by stable fingerprint, so the same trend day-over-day reuses its row and its cached derivations. Trends that stop appearing age out and are eventually retired. Refresh runs take a claim so two cannot overlap.

Quotable Quotes draws on a second, narrower input: an external dialogue popularity signal, used strictly to weight lines that have already circulated. It’s optional by design, so if the signal is unavailable a line gets no boost rather than failing the job.

The QuickSearch job layer

This layer is where a single selection becomes a retrieval strategy. It executes each action asynchronously and returns a ranked set of clips.

  • Request path – The web application is a React single-page application served from Amazon S3 through Amazon CloudFront. Its API is a Fastify service running on AWS Lambda behind an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API, with Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition for relational data.
  • Asynchronous execution – Selecting a QuickSearch action writes a job record to Amazon DynamoDB and enqueues an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) message. A worker Lambda function picks it up and runs the pipeline for that action. Transient failures retry through Amazon SQS, and errors classified as non-retriable go straight to a dead-letter queue.
  • Query formulation – Each action expands into a set of retrieval queries shaped by its editorial criteria. For Trend Align, this is where most of the proprietary work sits: A trend arrives as a cultural topic, and what a video index can match is what appears on screen and in the audio. Bridging those two is a translation problem, which Claude models on Amazon Bedrock handle. The output is a set of queries the index can act on.
  • Multi-channel retrieval – Each query goes to the search Lambda function, which handles hybrid retrieval. Marengo embeds the query once, as text, an image, or a composed text-plus-image query. The embedded query then executes across six k-NN channels (visual, audio, transcript, on-screen text, scene description, and labels) and seven BM25 text channels. Per-modality weights come from the query itself. Query-type routing adjusts channel boosts so dialogue queries lean on transcript and emotion channels while visual queries suppress them.
  • Fusion and reranking – The channels are combined with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which uses rank positions rather than raw scores and so avoids the scale mismatch between k-NN and BM25 similarity. The top candidates then pass through the Amazon Rerank model, a cross-encoder called through the Rerank API in Amazon Bedrock, for a final text-to-text relevance pass, followed by a Claude validation step over the top results.
  • Aggregation – The index stores short fixed-length clips. Before results are returned, adjacent clips with high visual-embedding similarity are merged into coherent moments, so a query for a scene returns one 20–60 second result rather than five fragments of the same scene.
  • Editorial ranking – A Claude model on Amazon Bedrock ranks the deduplicated, enriched candidates against the action’s editorial criteria. The pool is capped so the model’s output can’t truncate. Model choice is per action: Claude Sonnet where cultural recall changes the answer, Claude Haiku where the task is bounded and cost-sensitive.
  • Frame extraction – For Memeable Moments, a dedicated Lambda function extracts several candidate frames from the winning clip and scores them for face quality using Amazon Rekognition and for image sharpness. It then re-extracts the winner at full resolution, trims letterboxing, and returns a signed Amazon CloudFront URL.
  • Caching – Completed results are stored in Amazon DynamoDB and reused for 30 days. The cache key includes a per-action pipeline version and, for Trend Align, a hash of the active trend set, so a criteria change, a model upgrade, or a refreshed trend catalog invalidates cleanly rather than serving a stale answer.

Design decisions

Three choices made culturally informed retrieval tractable.

Separating trend acquisition from content understanding

A library changes when new content is added. Trends change daily, and early-stage trends faster than that. Coupling the two would mean either reprocessing content against fresh signal, which is computationally untenable, or serving stale trend judgment. Keeping them as independent pipelines joined at request time means signal stays current without the library ever being touched again. A title that finished airing years ago can re-enter a live conversation.

Splitting each action into cheap retrieval and expensive judgment

The naive design puts one large model in front of the whole library. QuickSearch instead uses inexpensive, high-recall vector and keyword retrieval to build a candidate pool, then spends model budget only on ranking a capped set of real candidates. The caps are sized against the ranking model’s output token limit, because a ranker that truncates mid-response silently drops results. This also keeps the per-query cost of Amazon Bedrock predictable: one embedding call, one rerank call, and a small fixed number of Claude invocations, regardless of library size.

Making cache invalidation an explicit editorial act

Results are cached for 30 days. Without intervention, a change to an action’s criteria or model would stay invisible to users until the cache expired. Each action carries a pipeline version that is bumped in the same change that alters its behavior. That bump invalidates prior results immediately, so editorial judgment is refined as a versioned change to the product rather than relitigated on every query.

Results

Social Department reports the following outcomes from customer use of QuickSearch. These are the company’s own observations rather than a controlled benchmark.

  • Queries that were previously impossible are now a single selection – Identifying the moments a fandom has canonized, or the frames that will function as memes for a specific audience, previously required a person with deep familiarity with the title watching footage, and it didn’t scale across a catalog.
  • Discovery no longer depends on manual scrubbing – According to Social Department, campaign discovery work that used to take 3–4 days now takes about 10 minutes with QuickSearch. The time a marketer spent scrubbing through episodes for the right moment goes back to higher-value campaign work.
  • Marketers reach candidate clips without composing a query – That removes the requirement that the person searching already knows the library well enough to describe what they want, the constraint that made discovery depend on the few people who had watched the show.
  • Archived catalog becomes addressable – Content that was effectively unreachable, because it was finished, archived, and invisible to metadata search, becomes usable for campaign work, and titles that stopped airing years ago can re-enter live cultural conversations.
  • Industry recognition – Social Department was showcased as a top startup at NAB 2026 and featured in the Entertainment Loft.

“The hard part here was never the search. It was working out what to search for: how you take something a great marketer does on instinct, about which moment lands and why, and turn it into criteria a system can execute a thousand times. We spent a long time on that. Working with TrackIt on a compressed timeline, we went from spec to a live demo at NAB. TwelveLabs gives us the intelligence to understand what’s inside the footage and AWS gives us the infrastructure to do it at library scale. Our job is to know what to point it at.”

— Jonathan Verk, Founder and CEO, Social Department

“Everyone in media talks about adding metadata to their libraries but tagging content doesn’t pay for itself. What I like about this project is that it closes the loop. It takes shows sitting in an archive and makes them useful for real campaigns, at a cost that makes sense to run every day. That’s the part the industry has been missing.”

— Chris Marchitelli, Vice President, TrackIt

What we learned

The following four lessons from the project stood out.

The hard problem was expressing judgment, not retrieving content

Retrieval is largely solved. What isn’t solved is specifying intent precisely enough for retrieval to be useful without an expert marketer in the loop. Most of the engineering effort went into defining what qualifies as a shareable scene or a memeable frame, tightly enough to execute repeatedly across libraries with different tones and audiences. That definition is the output of a standing evaluation program of numbered iterations, each measured against per-show ground-truth sets and a tracked baseline, that tunes the criteria against results rather than intuition.

A multi-model architecture on Amazon Bedrock

QuickSearch uses a multi-model architecture, with each model assigned to the work it fits best. Claude Haiku handles bounded, cost-sensitive output, and Claude Sonnet handles tasks where cultural recall changes the answer. TwelveLabs Marengo produces multimodal embeddings, TwelveLabs Pegasus provides scene-level video reasoning, and the Amazon Rerank model handles reranking. Amazon Bedrock made this architecture practical to build and run. Models from TwelveLabs, Anthropic, and Amazon are available through one API, so Social Department can change the model behind a task when measured quality moves, without building a new integration. Asynchronous invocation runs long video embedding jobs at library scale, and the Rerank API adds a relevance pass without separately hosted infrastructure. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails helps screen search input in the same service, and customer data stays within the AWS data boundary. Because Amazon Bedrock is fully managed, the team operates no model-serving infrastructure of its own.

Signal that decays needs its own architecture

Treating trend data as another input to the content pipeline would have failed, because the two have incompatible lifecycles. Recognizing early that library content and live culture are separate systems, with separate refresh rates, storage, and failure modes, was the decision the rest of the design depended on.

Clear layer boundaries made a multi-party project work

Social Department owned the pipeline architecture, retrieval system, and editorial criteria. TrackIt built and delivered against that architecture, and TwelveLabs supplied the video understanding models. AWS, with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, provided the infrastructure, model access, and solution architecture for the AWS components. Because each party had a clearly defined scope, the 8-week production timeline held.

Conclusion

We described how Social Department, working with TrackIt, TwelveLabs, and AWS, built culture-aware video discovery for entertainment marketing using its own pipeline and retrieval architecture. Several AWS components make up the layer this post describes. TwelveLabs Marengo handles multimodal embedding and TwelveLabs Pegasus handles scene-level video reasoning, both on Amazon Bedrock. Anthropic’s Claude models on Amazon Bedrock handle interpretation and editorial ranking, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless handles hybrid retrieval. AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, AWS Elemental MediaConvert, Amazon Rekognition, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon SQS run the pipelines around them. The result is a set of single-action queries that return the clips audiences already care about, the lines they already quote, the frames that will work as memes, and the moments that connect to whatever is trending right now.

To get started with multimodal video understanding on AWS, explore Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Service. To learn more about the TwelveLabs models available on Amazon Bedrock, visit the TwelveLabs page on AWS Marketplace. To explore how the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center can help your organization, visit the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center page.

Acknowledgements: The authors would like to thank Katie Kenney, Pranay Duhan, Xiaoye Qian, Rinne Han, and Dahler Battle for their work on this solution. We would also like to thank the TrackIt and TwelveLabs teams for their support.

entries.title: Connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to private APIs in a hub-and-spoke network with centralized inspection
entries.summary: Many enterprises run a centralized network model: one account owns every VPC and a central firewall inspects all traffic. This post shows a tested pattern for connecting Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to private APIs and MCP servers in that model, with the VPC Lattice resource gateway in the network account so every hop crosses the firewall.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to private APIs in a hub-and-spoke network with centralized inspection

In many enterprises, a central network team owns every virtual private cloud (VPC) and subnet, and every flow between VPCs must pass a central firewall in both directions. Agents that call internal REST APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, must meet the same two requirements. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model.

This post shows a pattern that meets both requirements. The network team keeps ownership of every subnet, and traffic between the Gateway and your private APIs and MCP servers crosses the central firewall in both directions. It covers where to place the Amazon VPC Lattice resource gateway that the Gateway uses to reach private targets. It also covers who owns each piece, six configuration decisions, and the checks that confirm the pattern works.

We built and tested the pattern in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region (

us-east-1
), in a lab with three member accounts and a management account in AWS Organizations. The AWS CloudFormation templates, test scripts, test evidence, and reference material (address plan, full validation checks, troubleshooting, quotas) are in the companion repository. Use the pattern as a guideline and adjust it to your own account architecture.

Terms used in this post

  • Resource gateway: The Amazon VPC Lattice entry point into a VPC: elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in subnets you choose. Backends see its addresses as the source of each connection.
  • Resource configuration: A VPC Lattice object that names one backend (here, an internal load balancer or VPC endpoint DNS name and port) behind a resource gateway. You can share it with other accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
  • Managed mode and self-managed mode: The two private endpoint options for Gateway targets. In managed mode, AgentCore creates the resource gateway for you. In self-managed mode, you create it and give the target a resource configuration.

When to use this pattern

Use this pattern when all of the following are true:

  • A network account owns every VPC, subnet, and AWS Transit Gateway attachment, and shares application subnets through AWS RAM.
  • A central firewall in an inspection VPC must inspect traffic entering and leaving every VPC.
  • Application teams manage only their own resources and security groups.

Otherwise, one of the options in Table 1 fits better.

Table 1: When another option fits better.

Your environmentUse
The Gateway account can own subnets that reach your toolsManaged mode
Traffic between the Gateway and the tools doesn’t need central inspectionSelf-managed mode, as documented
Tools are reachable on public endpointsA standard Gateway target

We also considered managed mode in subnets that AgentCore owns, a resource gateway in each tool VPC or in the central endpoints VPC, and internet-facing load balancers with AWS WAF per tool. The alternatives write-up explains why each falls short under these constraints.

Design requirements for centralized inspection

  • The network account owns every subnet. The Gateway and application accounts build only in subnets shared to them through AWS RAM.
  • Every flow between VPCs crosses the central firewall, in both directions. The central firewall in the inspection VPC inspects the traffic between the Gateway and your private APIs and MCP servers.

AgentCore Gateway reaches private targets through a VPC Lattice resource gateway, and the two private endpoint modes place it differently. Managed mode creates it in the Gateway account, which fits environments where that account can own the subnets it runs in. Self-managed mode, as documented, places it in subnets with direct access to the backend, which fits environments that do not require inspection between the Gateway and the tool. This environment needs both conditions at once, so the pattern uses self-managed mode with one change. The network account owns the resource gateway and places it in subnets routed through AWS Transit Gateway, so every request and reply passes the inspection VPC.

Solution overview

Give the resource gateway its own VPC and subnets in the network account. Don’t share them, and keep backends out of them. Route them through the transit gateway so every request and reply between VPCs crosses the firewall. Share one resource configuration per backend with the AgentCore account through AWS RAM. Figure 1 shows the accounts, VPCs, and traffic path.

Traffic path

  • The agent, in a shared subnet with no internet route, calls the Gateway URL. Private DNS on the Gateway interface endpoint resolves it inside the agent’s VPC.
  • AWS WAF, if attached, evaluates the request. The Gateway checks its resource policy and the inbound JSON Web Token (JWT), then picks the target and tool.
  • The Gateway gets an outbound OAuth token for the tool account and sends the request through VPC Lattice to the resource gateway in the network account.
  • The resource gateway subnets route to the transit gateway, which sends the traffic through the inspection VPC to the tool account’s internal Application Load Balancer (ALB) or 
    execute-api
    endpoint. (Crosses the firewall.)
  • The ALB or Amazon API Gateway validates the token and forwards the request to the backend.
  • The response returns the same way. (Crosses the firewall.)

How does Gateway traffic enter the network account’s VPC without a transit gateway attachment in the AgentCore account? When you create a target, AgentCore associates the shared resource configuration with its own VPC Lattice service network. VPC Lattice then delivers connections from that service network to the resource gateway’s network interfaces in your VPC. AWS operates that hop, and from there your routes and firewall take over.

What this pattern doesn’t do. Check these limits against your requirements before you adopt it:

  • No payload inspection – Traffic is TLS end to end from the Gateway to the ALB, with a certificate the Gateway validates. The firewall sees flow metadata and the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), not payloads. Request content is in the Gateway, AWS WAF, and ALB logs.
  • Some legs skip the firewall – The agent-to-interface-endpoint leg and the Gateway-to-resource-gateway leg don’t cross it. Neither do the token requests that AgentCore makes to each identity provider.
  • No end-user identity at the tool – With the client credentials grant, every call that reaches the tool carries the Gateway’s client identity. To trace a call to a caller, use the inbound JWT claims in the Gateway application logs.

Who owns what

Table 2: Who creates what.

One timeNew API on a connected ALBNew ALB or tool account
Network teamResource gateway and its VPC, subnets, and routes. Firewall rules. A default route from the tool VPC to the transit gateway for the ALB’s signing-key fetch. Gateway interface endpoint and policy. AWS RAM shareNothingOne resource configuration added to the share. A firewall rule if the range is new
Tool teamAn ALB certificate whose subject alternative name matches the target host name that the AgentCore team usesA listener rule (with 
jwt-validation
) on their ALB		 An internal ALB and security group, and an app client for the Gateway (client credentials grant, with a scope such as 
tools/invoke
)
AgentCore teamGateway, inbound authorizer, resource policy, optional AWS WAFOne Gateway target per API or MCP serverA target, plus an OAuth credential provider for a new identity provider

A new operation or tool on an existing target needs no new target: update the OpenAPI spec with 

UpdateGatewayTarget
, or call 
SynchronizeGatewayTargets
for an MCP server. The repository’s build order lists the steps in each account and the values the teams pass to each other.

Prerequisites

  • An organization in AWS Organizations with resource sharing in AWS RAM enabled.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) 2.37.7 or later, or the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) 1.43.106 or later, for the 
    certificateConfigurations
    parameter.
  • For the role that creates Gateway targets: 
    vpc-lattice:GetResourceConfiguration
    , 
    vpc-lattice:CreateServiceNetworkResourceAssociation
    , 
    vpc-lattice:GetServiceNetworkResourceAssociation
    , 
    vpc-lattice:ListServiceNetworkResourceAssociations
    , and 
    vpc-lattice:AssociateViaAWSService
    , plus the bedrock-agentcore target actions. Check your service control policies (SCPs) if your organization doesn’t use VPC Lattice today.
  • A firewall in a central inspection VPC attached to the transit gateway with appliance mode enabled.

Key design decisions

The snippets are excerpts from the lab templates and use the lab’s address plan. 

RGW_NET
is the resource gateway subnets (10.0.1.0/24–10.0.3.0/24), 
TOOL_NET
is the tool VPC (10.12.0.0/16), and 
ALB_NET
is the ALB subnets in it.

Decision 1: Put the resource gateway in a dedicated VPC in the network account

Create a dedicated VPC in the network account for the resource gateway, with subnets you don’t share and no central endpoints or backends. Route those subnets to the transit gateway. Keep one resource gateway per trust zone.

Used only with AgentCore, the resource gateway consumes one IP address per subnet, so small subnets are enough. Two settings can’t be changed after creation, 

Ipv4AddressesPerEni
and 
ResourceConfigDnsResolution
, so choose them up front. Use Availability Zone IDs that VPC Lattice and your AgentCore features support. The lab layout lists them for 
us-east-1
.

Decision 2: Create one resource configuration per load balancer, and share it through AWS RAM

Point the resource configuration at the internal ALB DNS name and share it with the AgentCore account. Don’t start the name with 

rcfg-
, which VPC Lattice reserves.

VPC Lattice delivers the connection to the resource configuration’s domain. AgentCore sends the target URL’s host name (for example 

tools.example.internal
) as the SNI and checks the ALB certificate against it. The certificate’s subject alternative name must match that host name. The host name doesn’t need to resolve in DNS.

For private API Gateway REST APIs, point one resource configuration at the network account’s 

execute-api
interface endpoint. Each API’s target uses its own URL, and each API’s resource policy must allow that endpoint through 
aws:SourceVpce
. In our tests, a second API in another account worked through the same resource configuration with no network change.

Decision 3: Pass only the flows you need through the firewall

Your firewall needs two stateful allows: from the resource gateway subnets to the tool VPC on port 443, and from the ALB subnets to the identity provider’s host name on port 443. Session-based firewalls pass replies of an allowed flow. In the lab we used AWS Network Firewall with strict rule order and the default actions Drop established and Alert established. With these defaults, the firewall drops client-to-server packets that no rule passes, and lets replies through unless a rule drops them. The rule-order notes explain the semantics.

The first rule allows only the resource gateway subnets to reach the tool VPC on port 443. The second allows the ALB to fetch its identity provider’s signing keys (JSON Web Key Set, or JWKS), only from the ALB subnets and only to the identity provider’s host name. The tool VPC needs a default route to the transit gateway for this fetch to reach central egress. If your identity provider isn’t Amazon Cognito, replace the host name. Without this rule, in our tests, the ALB returned HTTP 500 and the agent received 

MCP invocation failed
.

To prove replies cross the firewall, we added a drop rule for the reply direction preceding the pass rule:

Tool calls then hung until timeout, and the firewall logged 

to_client
drops for sid 100098. Removing the rule restored the calls. Run the same test on your own firewall.

Decision 4: Validate the tool account’s token on the internal ALB or private API

The tool account keeps its own identity provider (Amazon Cognito in the lab) and creates an app client for the Gateway. Validate that client’s token on every path to the backend.

Internal ALB – Make the listener’s default action a fixed response, and put a jwt-validation action on every rule that forwards. Pin 

client_id
to the Gateway’s app client so that other clients in the same user pool are rejected.

In our tests, a target with no token, one with another identity provider’s token, and one with a different app client’s token were all rejected with HTTP 401 before the backend ran. The agent saw only 

An internal error occurred
, so use the ALB access logs to diagnose token problems.

Private REST API – An API key doesn’t authenticate the caller, so add an authorizer to every method, such as a Cognito user pool authorizer with a required scope (as in the lab). Also attach an endpoint policy to the 

execute-api
endpoint that limits it to APIs owned by approved accounts. It controls which APIs the endpoint reaches, not who calls it. The authorizer controls the caller.

The ALB or endpoint security group allows only the resource gateway subnets, so the resource gateway is the only network path in. If your firewall applies source NAT, the security group must allow the firewall’s addresses instead, and it then admits anything the firewall forwards. The firewall rule and the token validation become the controls.

Decision 5: Create Gateway targets that reference the shared resource configuration

Create the Gateway with a JWT authorizer and, optionally, an AWS WAF web access control list (web ACL), which inspects the tool-call arguments for every target. AWS WAF inspects only the first 16 KB of the body by default (adjustable to 64 KB), so decide how each rule handles larger bodies. Add 

AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet
to the common rule set. See the AWS WAF notes.

Gateway targets with a private endpoint can’t use NO_AUTH for inbound authorization unless you configure an interceptor function.

Each target needs an OAuth credential provider that holds the tool account’s app client ID and secret and the identity provider’s discovery URL:

If the ALB uses a certificate from a private certificate authority (CA), also store the CA certificate as a PEM string in an AWS Secrets Manager secret. The Gateway execution role (the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role you give the Gateway when you create it) needs permission to read that secret and the credential provider.

An OpenAPI target uses the same blocks with 

openApiSchema
in place of 
mcpServer
. To rotate the CA, update the secret and call 
UpdateGatewayTarget
. Open connections can keep the old trust material for up to 15 minutes.
